hits.source: J. Comb. Theory, Ser. A 48, No. 2, 147-155 (1988).
hits.text: Two d-polyhedra in \(E^ d\) are nearly-neighborly if they are separated by a hyperplane which contains a facet of each. The main result is: there can be at most 15 mutually nearly-neighborly tetrahedra in \(E^ 3\). There is a glossary of results on nearly-neighborly (and neighborly) sets of polyhedra, several conjectures, relevant results on decomposition of certain graphs. The paper ends with the following ``Note added in proof. Using a similar yet more detailed approach, S. Furino, B. Gamble and J. Zako (sic) proved that there can be at most 14 nearly-neighborly tetrahedra in \(E^ 3\).''

hits.title: Putting convex \(d\)-polytopes inside frames
hits.source: J. Geom. 109, No. 2, Paper No. 32, 9 p. (2018).
hits.text:
A family \(\{P_1,\dots,P_k\}\) of convex \(d\)-polytopes in \(E^d\) is called neighborly if \(\dim(P_i\cap P_j)=d-1\) for \(i\not=j\), and nearly-neighborly if each pair \(P_i,P_j\), \(i\not= j\), can be separated by a hyperplane \(H\) with \(\dim(H\cap P_i)=\dim (H\cap P_j)=d-1\). 

The author develops several constructions for neighborly or nearly-neighborly families. The following are examples of the obtained results. For every \(m\geq 0\), there exists in \(E^{m+2}\) a nearly-neighborly family consisting of \(9\cdot 4^m\) members which are combinatorially equivalent to the \((m+2)\)-box. For all \(d\geq 2\), there exists in \(E^d\) a neighborly family consisting of \(3\cdot 2^{d-1}\) members which are prisms over the \((d-1)\)-simplex. For every \(m\geq 1\), there exists in \(E^{d+m}\) a neighborly family consisting of \(3\cdot 2^{d+m-1}\) members which are \(m\)-fold prisms over the \(d\)-simplex. Also some bounds are obtained.

Two neighborly families of 3-pyramids and of 3-boxes in \(E^{3}\)
hits.source: J. Geom. 109, No. 2, Paper No. 36, 5 p. (2018).
hits.text: A family \(\mathcal{P} = \{P_1,\dots,P_n\}\) of \(d\)-dimensional convex polytopes in Euclidean \(d\)-space is called \textit{neighborly} if, for each \(P_i\) and \(P_j\) with \(i \neq j\), the intersection \(P_i \cap P_j\) is a facet of both \(P_i\) and \(P_j\). It is known that a neighborly family of tetrahedra in \(E^3\) has at most eight tetrahedra, and that a neighborly family of \(3\)-pyramids has at most \(31\) pyramids. In this article, the author produces a neighborly family of sixteen \(3\)-pyramids, and a neighborly family of twenty-four combinatorial \(3\)-boxes.

The result of the convexification, obviously, is only a ``weakly convex'' or a ``nearly convex'' polygon which is contained in the boundary of its convex hull or which is a subdivision of a segment.

hits.text:
The article deals with the extension of the well-known problem in Euclidean 3D space. The extension is stated in the Theorem:

 If \(A=A_1, A_2,\dots, A_n\) and \(B_1,B_2,\dots, B_m\) is a split of the \(n+m=d+1\) vertices of a \(d\)-dimensional simplex in \(E^d\) into two non-empty disjoint sets, then there exist two parallel hyperplanes \(\pi\) and \(\sigma\), such that the set \(A\) is in the hyperplane \(\pi\) and the set \(B\) is in the hyperplane \(\sigma\) and the intersection \(\pi \cap \sigma\) is included in the hyperplane at infinity.

 One can split the vertex set of a \(d\)-simplex in \(E^d\) into more than two non-empty subsets. We get the following generalization: If the \(d + 1\) vertices of a \(d\)-simplex in \(E^d\) are split into \(k\) mutually-disjoint non-empty subsets \(A^1=A_1,1, A_1,2,\dots\), \(A^2= A_2,1, A_2,2,\dots\), \dots, \(A^k= A_k,1, A_k,2,\dots\) then there exist \(k\) hyperplanes \(\pi_1\), \(\pi_2\), \dots, \(\pi_k\), such that \(A^i\) is in \(\pi_i\) for all \(i\), and the intersection of all the hyperplanes is an affine flat at infinity of the suitable dimension.

hits.text:
Extending known results substantially the author proves the following three beautiful theorems. Suppose that \(f\) maps the \(d\)-dimensional rational space \(Q^d\) into itself.

 I. If \(f\) preserves distance \(\sqrt{2}\), then it must be an isometry, provided \(d\) is even and \(d\geq 6\), or \(d= 4k^2- 1\), for \(k\geq 2\).

 II. Preserving again distance \(\sqrt{2}\), \(f\) must preserve distance 2, provided \(d\geq 5\).

 III. If \(f\) preserves distances 1 and \(\sqrt{2}\), it must be an isometry, provided \(d\geq 5\).

hits.title: The Beckman-Quarles theorem for rational spaces
hits.text: The Beckmann-Quarles theorem asserts that for \(d > 1\) every mapping from a \(d\)-dimensional real space \(R^d\) into itself preserving the unit distance (`unit-preserving', i.e. pairs of points with distance 1 will be mapped into pairs of points, again with distance 1) will preserve any distance and hence is an isometry. For the rational case \(Q^d\) the same proposition is not a foregone conclusion. For some numbers \(d\) the matter has already been settled; the author adds the proof for the case of dimensions \(d = 2 n^2-1\) for \(n > 2\). This proof is indeed versatile as it can also be applied to several other cases.

Let \(S\subseteq R\). Then by \(G(S^ d)\) we denote a graph whose vertices are all the points of the real space \(R^ d\) with their coordinates in S and two vertices are connected by an edge if their distance is 1. 


In the paper it is proved that G(Q(\(\sqrt{k})^ d)\) is connected for all \(k\in N\), \(d\geq 5\); G(Q(\(\sqrt{k})^ 2)\) has countably infinitely many connected components for \(k=1,2,3,5,6(mod 8)\), and that for every algebraic number a, \(G(Q(a)^ d)\) is a connected graph for every large d.

The author proves: if \(n \in A\) and \(x,y \in \mathbb Q^n\), then there exists a finite set \(\{x,y\} \subseteq S_{xy} \subseteq \mathbb Q^n\) such that for every unit-distance preserving mapping \(f:S_{xy} \to \mathbb Q^n\), \(\|f(x)-f(y)\|=\|x-y\|\) holds.

hits.text: Parsons graphs are introduced with respect to the problem of finding the maximal set of matrices \(A_ 1,\dots,A_ m\) over a finite field with property \(\text{det} (A_ i)=1\) for all \(1\leq i\leq m\) and \(\text{det} (A_ i-A_ j)=1\) for all \(1\leq i<j\leq m\). The vertex set of a Parson graph \(T_ b(d,q)\) is the collection of all \(d\times d\) matrices \(A\) (\(d\) is even) over a finite field \(F\) with \(q\) elements for which \(\text{det} (A)=1\). Two vertices \(A\), \(B\) are adjacent in \(T_ b(d,q)\) iff \(\text{det} (A-B)=b\). There are shown some important properties of \(T_ b(d,q)\) as the vertex transitivity and some facts about the structure of these graphs. For the case \(b=0\) it is shown connectivity for all \(d\geq 4\). The author conjectures that every Parsons graph except for \(T_ 1(2,2)\) is connected and for \(d=2\), \(q\geq 3\) \(T_ b(d,q)\) has a 1-factor and is Hamiltonian.

hits.title: Monohedrally knotted tilings of the 3-space
hits.text:
A tiling by congruent copies of a single tile is called a monohedral tiling. The following theorem is from an unpublished example of P. McMullen. 


Theorem 1. For any polyhedral knot \(K\) in \({\mathbf E}^3\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists a tile \(M\) which is isotropic to an \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood of \(K\) such that \(M\) tiles \({\mathbf E}^3\) monohedrally. 


Zaks gives an elegent, one page construction that proves the following generalization. 


Theorem 2. Let \(G\) be a connected graph and \(f : G\rightarrow {\mathbf E}^3\) any piecewise linear embedding of \(G\) into \({\mathbf E}^3\). For any \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists a tile \(M\) which is isotropic to an \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood of a set \(H\), isotropic to \(f(G)\), such that \(M\) tiles \({\mathbf E}^3\) monohedrally.

hits.title: On the products of cross-ratios on diagonals of polygons. A short note
hits.text:
Let \(P = (V_1, V_2, \dots, V_n)\), \(V_{n + i} = V_i\), be a polygon in the plane, and let the diagonal \(V_i V_{i + 2}\) meet the diagonal \(V_{i + 1} V_{i + 3}\) at the point \(D_{i + 1} (1 \leq i \leq n)\). The points \(D_i\) are vertices of a new polygon \(\delta (P)\). This is the diagonal construction mentioned by \textit{B. Grünbaum} in ibid. 4, No. 1, 11-16 (1994; see the paper above). Let \(\rho (P)\) denote the product of all the cross-ratios on the diagonals of \(P\): \(\rho (P) - \prod_i (V_i, V_{i + 2}; D_i, D_{i + 1})\). Grünbaum conjectured that \(\rho (\delta (P)) = \rho (P)\).


A similar conjecture was raised by the author for a more general diagonal construction: For a fixed \(k\), \(k \geq 2\), and every \(i\), the diagonal \(V_i V_{i + k}\) intersects the diagonal \(V_{i + 1} V_{i + k + 1}\) at the point \(D_{i + 1}\); and let \(\rho (P) = \prod_i (V_i, V_{i + k}; D_i, D_{i + 1})\). Here the author proves \(\rho (\delta (P)) = \rho (P)\) in an even more general case, where for any fixed \(a \neq b\), and every \(i\), \(D_{i + b}\) is defined as the intersection of the diagonals \(V_i V_{i + a}\) and \(V_{i + b} V_{i + b + a}\), and \(\rho (P) = \prod_i (V_i, V_{i + a}; D_i D_{i + b})\), by giving an explicit expression for \(\rho (P)\).

hits.title: Neighborly families in \(E^d\) consisting of either \(d\)-pyramids over \((d-1)\)-cubes, or else of \(d\)-cubes
hits.source: J. Geom. 109, No. 3, Paper No. 46, 6 p. (2018).
hits.text:
A family \(\mathcal{P} = \{P_1,\dots,P_n\}\) of \(d\)-dimensional convex polytopes in Euclidean \(d\)-space is called \textit{nearly neighborly} if, for each \(P_i\) and \(P_j\) with \(i \neq j\), there exists a hyperplane separating \(P_i\) and \(P_j\) such that, for both \(P_i\) and \(P_j\), the intersection of the polytope and the hyperplane is a facet of the polytope. A stronger condition is to have \(P_i \cap P_j\) be a facet of both \(P_i\) and \(P_j\). When this happens, the family is called \textit{neighborly}.

The authors discuss two objects that may or may not exist for a nearly neighborly family, called \textit{common piercing lines} and \textit{rods}. Intuitively, a \(d\)-rod of \(\mathcal{P}\), which we denote \(R(\mathcal{P})\), is a combinatorial cube containing all of the polytopes in \(\mathcal{P}\) such that \(R(\mathcal{P})\) has two disjoint facets, \(B\) and \(T\), called the ``bottom'' and the ``top,'' with the following two properties: for each \(P \in \mathcal{P}\), there are facets \(F_B, F_T\) for which \(F_B \subset B\) and \(F_T \subset T\); and there exist lines \(\ell_B\) and \(\ell_T\) such that \(\ell_B\) passes through the interiors of all of the \(F_B\) and \(\ell_T\) passes through the interiors of all of the \(F_T\).

Given a nearly neighborly family, there is not necessarily a rod. However, in the article under review, the authors prove that for each \(d \geq 3\), there does exist a neighborly family of \(d\)-polytopes in Euclidean \(d\)-space which has a rod. This family consists of \(2^d\) convex combinatorial cubes, and is proven by induction. While the proof is short, the authors provide five corollaries, regarding neighborly families of \(d\)-cubes, neighborly tetrahedra in \(3\)-space, and existence of common piercing lines.

hits.text:
Let \(A=(a_{ij})\) be an \(m\times n\) matrix for which \(\{a_{i1},a_{i2},...,a_{in}\}=\{1,2,...,n\}\) for all i, 1\(\leq i\leq n\); let \(\sigma_{ij}\) be the permutation obtained by using the i-th and the j-th row of A, i.e. \(\sigma_{ij}(a_{it})=a_{jt}\) for all t, 1\(\leq t\leq n\). Let \(c_{ij}\) denote the number of cycles in the permutation \(\sigma_{ij}\). A simple proof is given to the Three Permutation Theorem [\textit{A. Kotzig}, Cas. Pestovani Mat. 83, 348-354 (1958; Zbl 0084.196)]: For all \(i\neq j\neq k\), \(c_{ij}+c_{jk}+c_{ki}\equiv n(mod 2).\) Consequently, if \(m=2s+1,\) then \(\sum_{i<j}c_{ij}\equiv sn(mod 2).\) 


The following two applications are derived: (I) Let G be an r-regular graph and let L be a proper edge-coloring of G by r colors; let c(G,L) denote the total number of cycles of G which are alternatingly colored by (any) two colors of L. If G is bipartite, r-regular, \(r=2s+1,\) and if G has 2n vertices, then for every coloring L c(G,L)\(\equiv sn(mod 2)\). A simple proof is obtained to the following theorem [\textit{A. Kotzig}, Proc. Symp. Smolenice 1963, 63-82 (1964; Zbl 0173.262)]: If G is a strongly hamiltonian r-regular graph, \(r\geq 3\), then \(| V(G)| \equiv 2(mod 4).\) 


(II): An intercalate in a latin square is a latin subsquare of order 2; let I(n) denote the maximum number of intercalates that a latin square of order n can have. We partially improve the upper bounds \(I(n)\leq n^ 2(n-1)/4\) for even n and \(I(n)\leq n(n-1)(n-3)/4\) for odd n, obtained by \textit{K. Heinrich} and \textit{W. D. Wallis} [Combinatorial Mathematics VIII, Proc. 8th Aust. Conf., Geelong/Aust. 1980, Lect. Notes Math. 884, 221-233 (1981; Zbl 0475.05014)], by showing that \(I(4k+1)\leq 2k(8k^ 2-4k-1)\) and \(I(4k+2)\leq(2k+1)(8k^ 2+1),\) for all \(k\geq 1\).

hits.title: Geometric permutations for convex sets
hits.text:
In connection with Helly's theorem about families of convex sets, much research has been devoted to the search for a similar theory concerning common transversals. The present paper may well be a major step toward such a theory: 


If A is a family of pairwise disjoint convex sets, and if the straight line G meets all members of A, then each of the two standard linear orderings of G induces an ordering of A. Let f(n) be the maximal possible number of pairs of orderings which can be induced in this way on any family A of pairwise disjoint convex sets in the Euclidean plane, and denote by g(n) the corresponding number for families of linesegments. The authors improve earlier bounds for f and show, by ingenious geometric arguments, that \(g(n)=n\), for every \(n\geq 3\). The paper ends with a number of open questions, also concerning the situation in higher dimensions.

Extending known results substantially the author proves the following three beautiful theorems. Suppose that \(f\) maps the \(d\)-dimensional rational space \(Q^d\) into itself.

In this interesting paper the authors pose some problems that arise from the following classical results: Theorem 1 (R. P. Boas jun., 1935). Suppose \(f\in C^{\infty}(I)\) where I is a real interval. Suppose further that, for some \(r>0\), the sequence \(r^ n(f^{(n)}(x)/n!)\) is bounded, for each \(x\in I\). Then f is analytic on I. Theorem 2 (E. Corominas and F. Sunyer Balaguer, 1954). Suppose \(f\in C^{\infty}(I)\). If, for each \(x\in I\), there is a nonnegative integer \(n=n(x)\) such that \(f^{(n)}(x)=0\), then f is a polynomial. 


In the paper under review multivariate analogues of both theorems are given as well as their improvements in rather different directions. 


Reviewer's remark: The authors conjecture the following: Suppose D is a connected open subset of \({\mathbb{R}}^ n\), \(f\in C^{\infty}(D)\) and that, for each \(x\in D\), there is some \(m=m(x)\in {\mathbb{N}}\) such that \(f^{\alpha}(x)=0\) for all \(\alpha \in {\mathbb{N}}^ n\) satisfying \(| \alpha | =n\). Then f is a polynomial. Note that this easily follows from Theorem 2 and from the fact that a function (on \({\mathbb{R}}^ n)\) that is a polynomial with respect to each variable separately must be a polynomial.

Summary: A subset \(S\) of an abelian group \(A\) is a forbidden set of translations (or is forbidden, for short) by a coloring of \(A\) if and only if \(a\) and \(a+s\) have different colors, for each \(a\in A\), \(s \in S\). Forbiddable sets play roles in certain approaches to various Euclidean Ramsey problems; this motivates the search for large forbiddable sets.


For each positive integer \(n\), each abelian group contains maximal sets forbiddable by an \(n\)-coloring of the group. In this study we deal mainly with the case \(n=2\). Suppose \(S\) is a maximal subset of \(A\) forbiddable by a 2-coloring of \(A\). Conclusions:


1. If \(s_ 1,\ldots,s_ k \in S\), \(m_ 1,\dots,m_ k\) are integers, and \(\sum m_ i\) is odd, then \(\sum m_ is_ i \in S\).


2. If \(A\) is a vector space over \(\mathbb{Q}\), then \(S\) is closed under multiplication by \({p \over q}\), whenever \(p\) and \(q\) are odd integers.


3. In case 2, \(A=(S+S) \cup S \cup( \bigcup^ \infty_{m=1}2^{-m}S)\), and the sets in this union are pairwise disjoint.


4. If \(A\) is a field containing \(\mathbb{Q}\), and \(S\) is maximal with respect to the conjunction of the properties of being two-forbiddable and being closed under multiplication, then \(S\) is closed under the operations mentioned in 1 and 2, above, under the taking of reciprocals, and under the taking of square roots, when they exist in \(A\). Further, every \(\alpha \in A \backslash S\) is a root of a polynomial \(p_ \alpha\) with coefficients in \(S \cup(S+S)\) satisfying \(p_ \alpha(s) \in S\) for all \(s \in S\).

Summary: [For the entire collection see Zbl 0747.00033.]


If the author's memory serves well, the parameter of the title was stumbled upon by the late Allen Shields and Frank Harary while they mused on a conjecture of the former. The Shields-Harary indices of vulnerability of a graph
hits.text:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph, \(I\subset [0,\infty)\) be an interval, \(f:I\to [0,\infty)\) be a nonincreasing function. For a function \(g: V\to I\), a set \(S\subset V\) is called \(g\)-admissible, if \(\sum_ {v\in V(H)} g(v)\leq 1\) holds for each component \(H\) of \(G-S\). Similarly, \(S\) is called strictly \(g\)-admissible, if the preceding inequality is strict for each \(H\). The Shields-Harary number of \(G\) is defined by \(\text{SH}(G,f)= \sup_g \min_{Sg\text{-admissible}}\sum_{v\in S} f(g(v))\). 


The Shields-Harary number measures a certain kind of fortifiability of graphs: it is the minimum cost incurred by removing a subset \(S\) of the nodes in such a way that the remaining components have small cumulative weight \(g\). For \(f(x)=1/x\) and the path \(P_n\) of \(n\) nodes, the assertion \(\text{SH}(P_n,f)\leq n\) is equivalent to a conjecture by Shields which has been proved by \textit{S. H. Schanuel} [Proc. Am. Math. Soc. 65, 185-186 (1977; Zbl 0368.05007)].


In the present paper, the authors study the quantity SH and some related indices: \(\overline{\text{SH}}(G,f)\) is defined in the same way as SH, but ``\(g\)-admissible'' is replaced by ``strictly \(g\)-admissible''. If the supremum is taken over all constant functions \(g: V\to I\), the corresponding quantities are called \(\text{SH}_0\) and \(\overline{\text{SH}}_0\), respectively.


It is proved that \(\text{SH}(G,f)=\overline{\text{SH}}(G,f)\) and \(\text{SH}_0(G,f)=\overline{\text{SH}}_0(G,f)\) if \(1\) is in the interior of the interval \(I\) and if \(f\) is continuous from the right at every point of \(I\cap[0,1]\).


Under suitable conditions, the supremum in the ``strict'' quantities is actually achieved; whereas under some other conditions, the supremum in the other quantities is not a maximum.


If \(1\) is in the interior of \(I\) and \(f\) is continuous from the right at each point of \(I\cap [0,1]\), then for each \(g:V\to I\) there is a set \(S\subset V\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V(H)} g(v)<1\) for each component \(H\) of \(G-S\), and \(\sum_{v\in S}f(g(v))\leq \text{SH}(G,f)\).


A further result shows that---under suitable conditions on \(I\) and \(f\)---for the constant functions \(g\), the quantities \(\text{SH}_0\) and \(\overline{\text{SH}}_0\) are achieved by constant assignments \(1/k\), \(k\in\{1,\dots, n\}\).


A set \(S\) is called minimally \(g\)-admissible if it is \(g\)-admissible and \(\sum_{v\in S} f(g(v))\) is minimum among all such sums over \(g\)-admissible sets of nodes. For a subset \(S\) of \(V\), let \(F(S)\) be the set of all \(g:V\to I\) such that \(S\) is minimally \(g\)-admissible. Then it is proved that \(\text{SH}(G,f)=\max_{S\subseteq V} \sup_{g\in F(S)} \sum_{v\in S} f(g(v))\). Similar results hold for the other indices.


Finally, bounds for some of the indices for the following graphs are given: the complete graph on \(n\) nodes, the star with \(n\) nodes, the path with \(n\) nodes and the cycle with \(n\) nodes.

hits.text: There are two well-known ways of defining the fractional chromatic number of a graph \(G\). One of them defines this parameter as the infimum of a certain linear program, the other makes use of set colorings of \(G\). In this note the author discusses the relationship of these two definitions and shows that they are equivalent if the fractional chromatic number of \(G\) is finite. Finally, he lists several interesting open problems with a particular emphasis on infinite graphs.

hits.title: The mathematical coloring book. Mathematics of coloring and the colorful life of its creators. Forewords by Branko Grünbaum, Peter D. Johnson jun., and Cecil Rousseau
hits.text:
This very nicely presented book, lovingly prepared by the author over a period of 18 years, studies problems involving colored objects, and the Ramsey theory that such problems are imbedded into. Two problems receiving special attention are the well-known four color problem (resolved in 1976 after an assault of 124 years) and the author's ``favorite open problem in mathematics'', the chromatic number of the plane problem: What is the smallest number of colors sufficient for coloring the plane so that no two points of the same color are unit distance apart? The book is very thorough, in unusual ways perhaps best expressed by the author himself: 


 
``This book includes not just mathematics, but also the process of investigation, trains of mathematical thought, and where possible, psychology of mathematical invention. The book does not just include history and prehistory of Ramsey theory and related fields, but also conveys the process of historical investigation -- the kitchen of historical research if you will. It has captivated me, and made me feel like a Sherlock Holmes -- I hope my reader will enjoy this sense of suspense and discovery as much as I have. \dots I hope the book will present mathematics as a human endeavor: the reader should expect to find in it not only results, but also portraits of their creators; not only mathematical facts, but also open problems; not only new mathematical research, but also new historical investigations; not only mathematical aspirations, but also moral dilemmas of the times between and during the two horrific World Wars of the twentieth century.''


 
For example, new facts and artifacts are presented, pertaining to the lives of Issai Schur, Pierre Joseph Henry Baudet, and Bartel Leendert van der Waerden. The 49 chapters are divided into 11 parts: I. Merry-go-round; II. Colored plane; III. Coloring graphs; IV. Coloring maps (a map is defined to be a plane connected multigraph with no bridges); V. Colored graphs; VI. The Ramsey principle; VII. Colored integers: Ramsey theory before Ramsey and its aftermath; VIII. Colored polygons: Euclidean Ramsey theory; IX. Colored integers in service of chromatic number of the plane; X. Predicting the future (here the author conjectures that the chromatic number of the plane is either 4 or 7, expressing a preference for 7); XI. Farewell to the reader. There are an extensive bibliography, and indices of names, subjects, and notations; the latter two are brief. The author has used his own book as a text, at both the senior and the graduate level. There are numerous open problems, but no formal problem sets. But there is much to recommend this book, both for mathematicians and for those who wish to learn more about mathematicians and their subject.

hits.title: The Colorado Mathematical Olympiad: The third decade and further explorations. From the mountains of Colorado to the peaks of mathematics. With forewords by Branko Grünbaum and Peter D. Johnson jun.
hits.text:
The book under review presents a year-by-year history of the Colorado Mathematical Olympiad from 2004 to 2013 with all the problems from the competitions and their solutions. Apart from its obvious historical and archival value, it serves as a vast repository of problems at the Olympiad level, useful both to students who want to prepare for the competition and to faculties looking for hard elementary problems. Moreover, this volume includes ten further explorations, bridges from solved Olympiad problems. The book is well conceived and developed and it contains more than just problems, solutions, and event statistics.

The reviewer considers that this book offers a great treasure of interesting problems, potential avenues of exploration and research for students, and new insights into solving elementary problems. No library will want to be without a copy, nor will anyone involved in mathematics competitions at this level.

hits.title: Hall's condition for list-coloring, and the Hall parameters: Recent developments
hits.text:
In a list colouring of a graph \(G\), each vertex \(v\) of \(G\) is assigned a list \(L(v)\) of ``permitted'' colours and it is required to find a colouring \(\phi\) of \(G\) such that for each vertex \(v\) one has \(\phi(v)\in L(v)\), and that adjacent vertices are assigned distinct colours. The list colouring number \(c(G)\) of \(G\) is the smallest integer \(m\) such that \(G\) can be list-coloured with respect to any list assignment where \(|L(v)|\geq m\) for each vertex \(v\). 


In 1988 \textit{A. J. W. Hilton} [J. Comb. Math. Comb. Comput. 3, 121-134 (1988; Zbl 0661.05025)] realized that list-colouring problems are strongly related to the area of systems of distinct representatives. A proper list-colouring can be thought of as a system of representatives of the system \((L(v))_v\) where the representatives are only required to be distinct when the corresponding vertices are adjacent. Moreover, \textit{A. J. W. Hilton} and \textit{P. D. Johnson} [Topics in combinatorics and graph theory. Essays in honour of Gerhard Ringel, 360-371 (1990; Zbl 0731.05017)] observed that Hall's marriage condition can be generalized in a natural way to graphs with list assignments. With this generalization, one can define the Hall number \(h(G)\) of a graph \(G\) to be the smallest positive integer among those \(m\) for which there exists an \(L\)-colouring of \(G\) whenever \(G\) and the list assignment \(L\) satisfy Hall's condition, and \(|L(v)|\geq m\). The paper surveys recent development of these ideas, covering such topics as critical graphs with respect to the Hall number, list-colourings with a restricted number of colours, multicolourings, and others.

hits.title: Another network vulnerability parameter
hits.text:
Summary: A weighted network is a pair \((G,w)\), in which \(G\) is a finite simple graph, and \(w\) a function assigning nonnegative weights to the vertices of \(G\). We say that (the removal of) a set \(S\subseteq V(G)\) dismantles \((G,w)\) iff the sum over any connected component of \(G-S\) of the values of \(w\) is less than \(1\).


The Shields-Harary family of parameters have to do with situations in which an enemy of the network suffers a cost for removing a vertex, the cost being a (non-increasing) function of the weight at that vertex. These parameters come out of weighting the network so as to maximize the cost of dismantling it.


Here is a different situation that seems more realistic, in warfare and economics: the enemy suffers no cost in removing a vertex but, on the other hand, the enemy has no knowledge of the network's structure and only a vague idea of its location. The enemy will knock out any vertex that it detects; the probability of detection is a non-decreasing function of the weight at the vertex. The aim is to minimise the probability of dismantling (or in other words, to maximise the chance that the network survives) by clever weighting of the vertices. We give a few basic results on this matter, and pose problems.

hits.title: Infinite graphs and the fractional chromatic number: Some recent surprises
hits.text: The author posed several questions in [Geombinatorics 5, No. 3, 99-108 (1996; Zbl 0856.05036)]. In [Geombinatorics 9, No. 1, 10-20 (1999)] he responded to those questions dealing with the origins of definitions of the fractional chromatic number. In the present essay, he responds to questions about the fractional chromatic number of infinite graphs, with emphasis on the relation between the fractional chromatic number of the full graph and the fractional chromatic number of finite subgraphs. The author relies heavily on \textit{E. R. Scheinerman} and \textit{D. H. Ullman} [Fractional graph theory (John Wiley \& Sons, New York) (1997; Zbl 0891.05003)].

hits.title: Problems posed in or arising from ``Colorings of metric spaces'': Status report
hits.text: The present article is a survey of results contained in the paper ``Colorings of metric spaces'' by \textit{M. Benda} and \textit{M. Perles} (written in 1976 and circulated in preprint form, but published only recently [Geombinatorics 9, No. 3, 113-126 (2000; Zbl 0951.05037)]), as well as some subsequent developments on open problems posed in it. Given a metric space \(X\) and a positive number \(r\), the graph \((X,r)\) has vertices the points of \(X\), with \(x\) and \(y\) joined by an edge iff the distance between \(x\) and \(y\) is \(r\). The problems discussed in the article are concerned primarily with determining the chromatic number and the connectivity of graphs of the form \((X,r)\). Specifically, (1) determine the chromatic number of \((Q^n,1)\) for \(n \geq 5\), and of \((X,1)\), when \(X\) is a finite algebraic extension of \(Q^2\), (2) characterize the subgroup of \(Q^n\) generated by the elements of length 1 (\((Q^n,1)\) is connected if and only if this group is all of \(Q^n\)), and similarly for \(F^n\), when \(F\) is a finite real algebraic extension of \(Q\) and (3) determine the connectivity of \((F^n,1)\), when \(F\) is either \(Q(\sqrt{n_1},\dots,\sqrt{n_t})\) with \(n_1,\dots,n_t \in Q\) or \(Q(\alpha)\), where \(\alpha\) is a real algebraic number.

hits.title: Graphs such that all minimum dominating sets intersect all maximally independent sets
hits.text: Motivated by a problem about the inverse domination number, \(DI\)-pathological graphs are introduced as the graphs in which every minimum dominating set intersects every maximally independent set. It is proved that if \(G\) is a connected \(DI\)-pathological graph with \(\gamma(G)=3\), then every vertex from a minimum dominating set \(D\) has at least two private neighbors in \(V(G)\setminus D\). Consequently the unique connected \(DI\)-pathological graph with \(\gamma(G)=3\) and with the least number of vertices and edges is found. Infinite families of the so-called exploded paths and exploded cycles are proved to be \(DI\)-pathological. (Explosion is also known in the literature as the X-join and was introduced in [\textit{G. Sabidussi}, Math. Z. 76, 385-401 (1961; Zbl 0109.16404)]).

hits.title: Edge colorings of complete multipartite graphs forbidding rainbow cycles
hits.source: Theory Appl. Graphs 4, No. 2, Article 2, 9 p. (2017).
hits.text: Summary: It is well known that if the edges of a finite simple connected graph on $n$ vertices are colored so that no cycle is rainbow, then no more than $n-1$ colors can appear on the edges. In previous work, it has been shown that the essentially different rainbow-cycle-forbidding edge colorings of $K_n$ with $n-1$ colors appearing are in $1-1$ correspondence with (can be encoded by) the (isomorphism classes of) full binary trees with $n$ leafs. In the encoding, the natural Huffman labeling of each tree arising from the assignment of 1 to each leaf plays a role. Very recently, it has been shown that a similar encoding holds for rainbowcycle-forbidding edge colorings of $K_{a,b}$ with $a+b-1$ colors appearing. In this case the binary trees are given Huffman labelings arising from certain assignments of $(0,1)$ or $(1,0)$ to the leafs. (Sibling leafs are not allowed to be assigned the same label.) In this paper we prove the analogous result for complete $r$-partite graphs, for $r>2$.

hits.title: Achieving metric dimension one by weighting the edges of a connected network
hits.source: Int. J. Math. Comput. Sci. 16, No. 1, 503-514 (2021).
hits.text: Summary: Metric dimension is a cardinal number that can be attached to any metric space. A metric space has metric dimension 1 if and only if for some point in the space, the distances from that point to the other points are all different.\par Attaching positive weights to the edges of a connected network naturally defines a metric on the node set of the network. In this paper we consider the following two optimization problems: given a connected network, attach positive integer weights to its edges so that the induced metric space has metric dimension one, and (i) the maximum of the assigned weights is as small as possible; or (ii) the sum of the assigned weights is as small as possible.

hits.title: Edge colorings of $K(m,n)$ with $m+n-1$ colors which forbid rainbow cycles
hits.source: Theory Appl. Graphs 4, No. 1, Article 1, 15 p. (2017).
hits.text: Summary: For positive integers $m$, $n$, the greatest number of colors that can appear in an edge coloring of $K_{m,n}$ which avoids rainbow cycles is $m+n-1$. Here these colorings are constructively characterized; it turns out that these colorings can be encoded by certain vertex labelings of full binary trees with $m+n$ leafs.

hits.title: Inequalities relating degrees of adjacent vertices to the average degree
hits.text: By a hypergraph with a fixed number of vertices (per edge), say n, the authors understand a matrix of non-negative integers with constant row sum n; they allow vertices to occur more than once in an edge. The authors prove a theorem from which they draw four corollaries. One of them states that the geometric degree of the vertices is not less than the arithmetic degree. Another corollary relates the number of edge, the number of vertices, and the largest number of triangles based on a fixed edge.

hits.title: On the Babai and upper chromatic numbers of graphs of diameter 2
hits.text: Summary: The Babai numbers and the upper chromatic number are parameters that can be assigned to any metric space. They can, therefore, be assigned to any connected simple graph. In this paper we make progress in the theory of the first Babai number and the upper chromatic number in the simple graph setting, with emphasis on graphs of diameter 2.

hits.title: A characterization of partition-good and partition-wonderful complete multipartite graphs
hits.source: Int. J. Math. Comput. Sci. 19, No. 3, 739-749 (2024).
hits.text: Summary: A simple graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices is partition-good if and only if for all pairs \((a,b)\) of positive integers such that \(a+b=n\), \(V(G)\) can be partitioned into sets \(A\), \(B\) satisfying: \(|A|=a\), \(|B|=b\), and \(G[A]\), \(G[B]\) are connected. \(G\) is partition-wonderful if and only if either (i) \(n=1\), or (ii) \(n>1\), \(G\) is connected, and of all pairs \((a,b)\) of positive integers such that \(a+b=n\), \(V(G)\) can be partitioned into sets \(A\), \(B\) satisfying: \(|A|=a\), \(|B|=b\), and \(G[A]\), \(G[B]\) are partition-wonderful. We characterize the partition-good and the partition-wonderful among the complete multipartite graphs, and, along the way, prove some elementary results about these graph properties.

hits.title: The new mathematical coloring book. Mathematics of coloring and the colorful life of its creators. With forewords by Peter D. Johnson Jun., Geoffrey Exoo, Branko Grünbaum, and Cecil Rousseau
hits.text:
Chromatic graph theory deals with coloring vertices, edges, or both of a graph \(G\) according to certain simple rules. However, the simplicity of the rules does not mean that the problems encountered are simple. Starting from the four-color problem around 1850, the theory has developed into a many-sided body of problems, theories, results, and applications. The number of simply stated but challenging problems remains large and growing.

The author's Mathematical coloring book (TMCB) was published in 2009 [The mathematical coloring book. Mathematics of coloring and the colorful life of its creators. Forewords by Branko Grünbaum, Peter D. Johnson jun., and Cecil Rousseau. New York, NY: Springer (2009; Zbl 1221.05001)]. It is now joined by the New mathematical coloring book (TNMCB), which is a colossal sibling of TMCB. This second edition of the book is a masterpiece, containing more than twice as much as the first edition. It includes striking results from the past fifteen years and solutions to problems from the first edition.

This very nicely presented book studies problems involving colored objects and the Ramsey theory. It mainly deals with the four-color problem and the author's favorite problem, namely, the chromatic number of the plane problem: What is the smallest number of colors needed for coloring the points of the plane in such a way that any two points at distance one receive two different colors? This book includes not just mathematics, but also the process of investigation. It is a unique combination of mathematics, history, and biography and the author has been intimately involved in the story for the last half-century. Mathematics is presented both as science and art and the author has set a standard for writing about mathematics and mathematicians that will be hard to match. The author engages the reader's attention not only mathematically, but emotionally and esthetically.

TNMCB consists of 68 chapters divided into 14 parts. I. Merry-go-round; II. Colored plane; III. Coloring graphs; IV. Coloring maps; V. Colored graphs; VI. The Ramsey principles; VII. Colored integers: Ramsey theory before Ramsey and its aftermath; VIII. Colored polygons: Euclidean Ramsey theory; IX. Colored integers in service of the chromatic number of the plane: how O'Donnell unified Ramsey theory and no one noticed; X. Ask what your computer can do for you XI. What about chromatic 6?; XII. Predicting the future; XIII. Imagining the real and realizing the imaginary; XIV. Farewell to the reader.

A large part of this new edition presents the most recent works by Auberg de Grey, Marijn Heule, Jann Parts, Geoffrey Exoo, and Don Ismailescu. New open problems and conjectures are included and this will lead to further work on the theme of this book. This book is strongly recommended to all those who wish to learn more about mathematics, mathematicians, the process of investigation and the psychology of mathematical invention.

hits.title: Constructively coloring the line
hits.text: Summary: \textit{A. Kemnitz} and \textit{M. Marangio} [Ars Comb. 85, 183--192 (2007; Zbl 1224.05175)] showed that for any list of \(k\) distances, the real line can be colored with \(k+1\) colors so that all \(k\) of the distances are ``forbidden'', meaning that two points any of those distances apart must be colored differently. Their proof is non-constructive, as it appeals to a famous theorem of \textit{N. G. de Bruijn} and \textit{P. Erdős} [Nederl. Akad. Wet., Proc., Ser. A 54, 371--373 (1951); Indag. Math. 13, 371--373 (1951; Zbl 0044.38203)],from the proof of which the axiom of choice cannot be excised. Here we give explicit instructions for obtaining distance-forbidding colorings, and raise questions about periodic colorings.

hits.title: Two-colorings of real quadratic extensions of \(Q^ 2\) that forbid many distances
hits.source: Combinatorics, graph theory, and computing, Proc. 18th Southeast. Conf., Boca Raton/Fl. 1987, Congr. Numerantium 60, 51-58 (1987).
hits.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0638.00009.] 


For an Abelian group \((A,+,0)\) with \(S\subseteq A\) the set S is called weakly two-free if \(\sum^{k}_{i=1}m_ is_ i\neq 0\) whenever \(s_ 1,...,s_ k\in S\) and \(m_ 1,...,m_ k\) are integers such that \(\sum^{k}_{i=1}m_ i\) is odd (*). A coloring of A forbids S if and only if, for all \(a\in A\) and \(s\in S\), a and \(a+s\) have different colors (**). Let \(G=G(A,S)\) be the Cayley graph, whose vertices are in A, and in which a,b\(\in A\) are adjacent if and only if a-b\(\in S\cup (-S).\) 


Then (*) says that S is weakly two-free if and only if there is no walk of odd length in G starting and ending at 0. Definition (**) says that a coloring of A forbids S if it is an admissible vertex-coloring of G. The content of the paper is the proof of the following theorem: 


Suppose that m is a squarefree positive integer, and \(m\equiv 1\) mod 4 or \(m\equiv 2\) mod 4. Then [Q(\(\sqrt{m})]\) 2 is two-colorable so that all the distances \(\sqrt{p/q}\), p, q odd positive integers, are forbidden. 


Further, the author poses some problems arising from this theorem.

hits.title: Scheduling $N$ burgers for a $k$-burger grill: chromatic numbers with restrictions
hits.source: Theory Appl. Graphs 2, No. 2, Article 3, 15 p. (2015).
hits.text: Summary: The chromatic number has a well-known interpretation in the area of scheduling. If the vertices of a finite, simple graph are committees, and adjacency of two committees indicates that they must never be in session simultaneously, then the chromatic number of the graph is the smallest number of hours during which the committees/vertices of the graph may all have properly scheduled meetings of one continuous hour each. \textit{T. Slivnik} [Extremal problems for cliques and colorings. Cambridge: University of Cambridge (PhD Thesis)  (1996)] showed that the fractional chromatic number can be similarly characterized. In that characterization, the meetings are allowed to be broken into a finite number of disjoint intervals. \par Here we consider chromatic numbers definable similarly, with the additional restriction that there are only $k$ meeting rooms available; that is, at each instant no more than $k$ committees can be in session.

hits.title: Greedy colorings and the Grundy chromatic number of the \(n\)-cube
hits.text: Let \(G\) be a graph and let \((v_1,v_2, \dots)\) be an ordering of its vertices. A greedy colouring of \(G\) colours the vertices of \(G\) by colours \(0,1,2, \dots\) in the order listed, and at the \(i\)th stage, the colour of \(v_i\) is defined to be the smallest colour not occurring on any neighbour of \(v_i\). The authors define the Grundy number \(\Gamma(G)\) of \(G\) to be the maximum, over all greedy colourings, of the number of colours used. It is easy to see that \(\Gamma(G)\leq\Delta(G)+1\), where \(\Delta(G)\) denotes the maximum degree of \(G\). The main result of the paper is that for the Grundy number of the \(n\)-dimensional cube \(Q_n\) one has \(\Gamma(Q_2)=2\) and \(\Gamma(Q_n) =n+1\), otherwise.

hits.title: Frankl's conjecture holds for topologies on finite sets
hits.text: Summary: Frankl's conjecture asserts that for any union-closed family \(\mathbb{F}\) of subsets of a finite set \(U\), some \(u\in U\) is an element of at least half of the sets in the family. Here we prove that Frankl's conclusion holds when \(\mathbb{F}\) satisfies the stronger requirement of being the collection of open sets of a topology on \(U\).

hits.title: A variation of Ryser's theorem and a necessary condition for the list- colouring problem
hits.source: Graph colourings, Proc. Conf., Milton Keynes/UK 1988, Pitman Res. Notes Math. Ser. 218, 135-143 (1990).
hits.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0693.05025.] 


For each edge e of a graph G, let C(e) be a set of colours; C(e) is the list for the edge e. A list colouring for a graph G is an edge colouring \(\phi\), such that \(\phi\) (e)\(\in C(e)\) for each edge e. The list colouring conjecture asserts that if \(| C(e)| \geq \chi '(G)\) for each edge \(e\in E(G)\), then G has a list colouring. The special case of the list colouring conjecture in which \(G=K_{n,n}\) is known as Dinitz' conjecture. In this paper an alternative version of Ryser's theorem is formulated and proved. The authors deduce an application of this theorem to the Dinitz' conjecture in the form of an inequality satisfied for each subgraph of a graph having a C-list colouring. Another conjecture about C-list colourings related to this inequality is proposed.

hits.title: Rainbow connectivity and proper rainbow connectivity of \(\theta(1,s,t)\)
hits.source: Int. J. Math. Comput. Sci. 16, No. 4, 1261-1277 (2021).
hits.text: Summary: A connected graph \(G\) is rainbow connected with respect to an edge coloring of \(G\) if each pair of distinct vertices of \(G\) are joined by a rainbow path -- a path with no color appearing on more than one edge of the path. \(G\) is strongly rainbow connected if each pair of distinct vertices of \(G\) are joined by a rainbow geodesic, a shortest path in \(G\) between the vertices. The (strong) rainbow connection number of \(G\), denoted (s)rc\((G)\), is the smallest number of colors in an edge coloring of \(G\) with respect to which \(G\) is (strongly) rainbow connected. \par We consider two recently introduced parameters, prc and psrc, defined as rc and src were, with the additional requirement that the edge colorings be proper. We mention some relations among the 4 parameters and evaluate them on some classes of graphs, including some of the theta graphs.

hits.title: Geometric etudes in combinatorial mathematics. With forewords to the 1st edition by Paul Erdős, Branko Grünbaum, and Cecil Rousseau. With new forewords to the 2nd edition by Branko Grünbaum, Peter D. Johnson jun. and Cecil Rousseau
hits.text:
The present second edition of this popular book for talented high school students and also for mathematicians contains mostly the material of the first edition. The contents of the first edition is outlined in the report (1991; Zbl 0727.52001).

The second edition is expanded by the following five short chapters. Chapter 5 (five pages) recalls two theorems by \textit{D. Karabash} [Geombinatorics 16, No.~2, 262--265 (2006)] on rectangles that can be tiled by L-tetrominoes of the same orientation in such a way that the tiling has \(2\)-fold symmetry. Chapter 6 (five pages) presents some results on three-dimensional tromino tilings of a cube obtained mostly by \textit{N. Starr} [Geombinatorics 18, No.~2, 72--87 (2008; Zbl 1184.05020)]. Chapter 7 (four pages) comments some results on the Ramsey number \(R(m,n)\), first of all the result by \textit{B. D. McKay} and \textit{S. P. Radziszowski} that \(R(4,5) = 25\) [J. Graph Theory 19, No.~3, 309--322 (1995; Zbl 0822.05050)], and also the estimates \(43 \leq R(5,5) \leq 49\) with the conjecture that \(R(5,5) =43\). See \textit{G. Exoo} [J. Graph Theory 13, No.~1, 97--98 (1989; Zbl 0661.05044)] and \textit{B. D. McKay} and \textit{S. P. Radziszowski} [J. Comb. Theory, Ser. B 69, No.~2, 193--209 (1997; Zbl 0860.05043)].

Chapter 8 (four pages) gives information on the progress in the research on the famous Borsuk problem after the first edition of this book; the story of finding counterexamples. Starting from the well-nown result by \textit{J. Kahn} and \textit{G. Kalai} [Bull. Am. Math. Soc., New Ser. 29, No.~1, 60--62 (1993; Zbl 0786.52002)] and finishing by the result of \textit{A. Hinrichs} and \textit{C. Richter} [Discrete Math. 270, No.~1--3, 137--147 (2003; Zbl 1028.52012)] on the counterexample in \(E^{298}\), which (till now) is the space of the lowest known dimension for which the Borsuk problem has a negative solution. 

Chapter 9 (twelve pages) discusses the following problem of E. Nelson (1950): which is the smallest number \(\chi\) of colours sufficient for colouring the plane in such a way that no two points of the same colour lie apart at unit distance. After recalling the proofs by E. Nelson (1950) and J. Isbell (1950) that \(4 \leq \chi \leq 7\), the author presents results on the \(n\)-colouring of a given type and on the almost chromatic number \(\chi_a\); see the paper by \textit{I. Hoffman} and \textit{A. Soifer} [Geombinatorics 3, No.~2, 38--40 (1993; Zbl 0845.05037)].

hits.title: On the independence numbers of the Van der Waerden and cyclic Van der Waerden hypergraphs \(W(k,t)\) and \(W_c(k,t)\) when \(t\) and \(k\) are powers of the same prime
hits.text: Summary: For integers \(1\le m<n\) and a prime \(p\) (we require \(2\le m\) when \(p=2)\), a subset \(I(p^n,p^m)\subseteq\{0,\dots,p^n-1\}\) is described which contains no \(p^m\)-term cyclic arithmetic progression modulo \(p^n\), and which is maximal among subset of \(\{0,\dots,p^n-1\}\) with that property.

hits.title: List multicolorings of graphs with measurable sets
hits.text: Summary: In an ordinary list multicoloring of a graph, the vertices are ``colored'' with subsets of pre-assigned finite sets (called ``lists'') in such a way that adjacent vertices are colored with disjoint sets. Here we consider the analog of such colorings in which the lists are measurable sets from an arbitrary atomless, semifinite measure space, and the color sets are to have prescribed measures rather than prescribed cardinalities. We adapt a proof technique of \textit{B. Bollobás} and \textit{N. T. Varopoulos} [Math. Proc. Camb. Philos. Soc. 78, 323--325 (1975; Zbl 0304.28001)] to prove an analog of one of the major theorems about ordinary list multicolorings, a generalization and extension of Hall's marriage theorem, due to \textit{M. Cropper}, \textit{A. Gyárfás} and \textit{J. Lehel} [J. Graph Theory 42, 246--255 (2003; Zbl 1011.05023)].

hits.title: Forbidding monochromatic odd cycles and rainbow cycles in complete graphs
hits.text: Summary: A \(k\)-edge coloring \(c\) of the edge set \(E (G)\) of a graph \(G\) is a surjective mapping \(c : E (G) \to [k] = \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}\). If \(\mathcal{F}\) and \(\mathcal{H}\) are families of graphs, \(\mathrm{MRS}(K_n; \mathcal{F}, \mathcal{H})\) is the set of numbers \(k\) such that there is a \(k\)-edge coloring of \(K_n\) with respect to which there is neither a monochromatic copy of any \(F \in \mathcal{F}\) nor a rainbow copy of any \(H \in \mathcal{H}\) in \(K_n\). Our main result is that for all \(n \geq 2\), \(\mathrm{MRS}(K_n;\{\text{odd cycles}\},\{\text{cycles}\}) = \{\lceil \log_2 n \rceil, \ldots, n - 1\} \). The proof will exploit an idea for edge-coloring connected graphs so as to forbid rainbow cycles to be found in \textit{D. Hoffman} et al. [Graphs Comb. 35, No. 6, 1585--1596 (2019; Zbl 1431.05068)].

hits.title: The closed neighborhood and filter conditions in solid sequence spaces
hits.source: Int. J. Math. Math. Sci. 12, No. 4, 625-632 (1989).
hits.text:
Summary: Let E be a topological vector space of scalar sequences, with topology \(\tau\) ; (E,\(\tau\)) satisfies the closed neighborhood condition iff there is a basis of neighborhoods at the origin, for \(\tau\), consisting of sets which are closed with respect to the topology \(\pi\) of coordinate-wise convergence on E; (E,\(\tau\)) satisfies the filter condition iff every filter, Cauchy with respect to \(\tau\), convergent with respect to \(\pi\), converges with respect to \(\tau\). 


Examples are given of solid normed spaces of sequences which (a) fail to satisfy the filter condition, or (b) satisfy the filter condition, but not the closed neighborhood condition. (Robertson and others have given examples fulfilling (a), and examples fulfilling (b), but these examples were not solid, normed sequence spaces.) However, it is shown that among separated, separable solid pairs (E,\(\tau\)), the filter and closed neighborhood conditions are equivalent, and equivalent to the usual coordinate sequences constituting an unconditional Schauder basis for (E,\(\tau\)). Consequently, the usual coordinate sequences do constitute an unconditional Schauder basis in every complete, separable, separated, solid pair (E,\(\tau\)).

hits.title: A geometric extremal result for cubic arrays
hits.text:
A set \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n}\) contains a right triangle if \(S\) contains three vertices of some right triangle. For a positive integers \(n\) and \(m\) denote by \([n]^m\) the set \(\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}^m\). An \(n\)-point subset of \([n]^m\), \(m \geq 2\), is called a coordinate line if \(m-1\) coordinates of these points are fixed. An upright triangle is a \(3\)-subset of \([n]^m\) such that there exist \(2\) its points lying in some coordinate line of \([n]^m\) and \(2\) its points lying in a different coordinate line of \([n]^m\). 


 
The authors prove that any subset of \([n]^2\), consisting of at least \(2n-1\) elements, contains an upright triangle. All \((2n-2)\)-element subsets of \([n]^2\) without upright triangles are characterized. An upper bound for the number of elements of the set \(S \subseteq [n]^m\), \(n,m \geq 2\), not containing upright triangles, is obtained. The greatest possible size of a subset of \([n]^3\) without upright triangles is calculated.

hits.title: Extending Hall's theorem
hits.source: Topics in combinatorics and graph theory. Essays in honour of Gerhard Ringel, 359-371 (1990).
hits.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0698.00017.] 


Suppose that to each vertex v of a finite simple graph G there is assigned a list C(v) of colours. The authors study the conditions for G and C(v) which guarantee that the vertices of G can be coloured so that each vertex v of G is coloured with a colour of C(v), and adjacent vertices are coloured differently. Such a colouring of G is called a C- colouring. 


The results are formulated using two definitions of Hall type: 


(i) A graph G with a vertex colour assignment \(C=C(v)\) satisfies Hall's condition if and only if for each subgraph H of G \(| V(H)| \leq \sum t(H,C),\) where it is summarized over all colours \(\sigma\) which occur in the assignment C, and t(H,C) denotes the maximum size of an independent set of vertices v in H for which \(\sigma\in C(v).\) 


(ii) A graph G with a colour assignment \(C=C(v)\) is called Hall(m) if and only if Hall's condition and the requirement \(| C(v)| \geq m\) for all vertices v of G suffice to ensure the existence of a C-colouring of G. 


Theorem 1: If G is a simple finite graph with vertex colour assignment C(v) and \(| C(v)| \geq \chi (G)\) for all vertices v of G, then G and C satisfy Hall's condition. 


Theorem 2: Every induced subgraph of a finite Hall(m) graph is Hall(m). 


Theorem 3: A simple graph G is Hall (i.e. both Hall(0) and Hall(1)) if and only if every block of G is a clique. 


In addition to this theorems, the authors give in Theorem 4 four examples which lead from a given list-colourable graph to a new list-colourable graph. (A graph G is list-colourable if and only if there exists a C- colouring of G for every vertex assignment C satisfying \(| C(v)| \geq \chi (G).)\) The paper ends with some remarks and problems. One of them is the conjecture: Every line graph is Hall(2).

hits.title: A pointwise condition for an infinitely differentiable function of several variables to be a polynomial
hits.text: In J. Math. Anal. Appl. 140, No.2, 301-309 (1989; Zbl 0684.26009) the authors proved the following extension of a theorem of E. Corominas and F. Sunyer Balaguer: Suppose that f is a \(C^{\infty}\) function on a connected, open subset D of \({\mathbb{R}}^ n\) such that for each x in D there is a nonnegative integer m(x) such that \(f^{\alpha}(x)=0\) for all multi-indices \(\alpha =(\alpha_ 1,...,\alpha_ n)\) satisfying \(| \alpha | =\alpha_ 1+...+\alpha_ n\geq m(x).\) Then f is a polynomial. They also conjectured that the theorem is true if one replaces the assumption that \(| \alpha | \geq m\) by the weaker one that \(| \alpha | =m.\) In the present note this conjecture is settled. (See also the reviewer's remark in the review cited above.)

hits.title: A very short proof of a well-known fact about circles in the plane
hits.text: Summary: The fact referred to in the title is that if \(C\) is a circle in the coordinatized real plane centered at a rational point and containing a rational point, then the rational points are dense on \(C\). From one well-known proof of this fact it can be deduced that for any two such circles, there is a homeomorphism of one onto the other that takes the rational points of the domain onto those of the range. From our proof it is obvious that there is such a correspondence arising from the composition of an isometry and a homothethic transformation of the plane.

hits.title: Functions which preserve unit distance
hits.text:
Starting point is the famous theorem by Beckmann and Quarles. In this note are contemplated and formulated some aspects and problems relative to the Beckmann-Quarles Theorem by variations of conditions.


One of the open questions is answered in the negative by \textit{A. Kuz'minykh} [ibid. 3, No. 4, 137-139 (1994; see the review below)].

hits.title: A function related to the Hall ratio
hits.text:
Summary: All graphs in this paper are both finite and simple. Let \(\alpha(G)\) denote the vertex independence number of a graph, \(G\). The Hall ratio of \(G\) is 
\[
\rho(G)= \max\Biggl\{{|V(H)|\over\alpha(H)}:H\text{ is a subgraph of }G\Biggr\}.
\]
 In general, finding the Hall ratio of a graph is, at best, a tedious task. In this paper, we define a function to aid us with this task and then observe how said function behaves on a variety of well-known graphs.

hits.title: On the secure-domination number of the full balanced binary tree
hits.source: Int. J. Math. Comput. Sci. 11, No. 2, 173-186 (2016).
hits.text:
Summary: The secure-domination number \(\gamma_s(G)\) of a finite simple graph \(G\) is the smallest size of a set of vertices in \(G\) which is both secure and dominating in \(G\). It is elementary that \(\frac {\gamma_s(G)}{|V(G)|}\geq\frac 12\). A currently unsolved problem:

 
Find the largest number \(g\in(\frac 12,1)\) such that there is a sequence \((H_n)\) of distinct connected graphs such that 
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac {\gamma_s(H_n)}{|V(H_n)|}=g.
\]
 
In early work on this problem the full balanced binary trees \(G_n\) (which has \(2^n\) leafs, each a distance \(n\) from the root vertex) were of interest. They are no longer, but the unexpected difficulty of determining \(\gamma_s(G_n)\) has made this determination of interest in itself. In this paper we show that 
\[
\lim\inf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\gamma_s(G_n)}{|V(G_n)|}\geq\frac{8}{15}
\]
 and give a construction of a secure-dominating set \(S_n\subseteq V(G_n)\) such that 
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{|S_n|}{V(G_n)}= \frac{11}{20}.
\]
 However, we find that \(S_n\) is not a minimum secure-dominating set in \(G_n\) for \(n\geq 6\).

hits.title: An anti-Waring conjecture and problem
hits.source: Int. J. Math. Comput. Sci. 6, No. 1, 21-26 (2011).
hits.text: The authors define the number \(N(k,r)\) to be the first integer such that it and every subsequent integer can be written as the sum of \(r\) or more distinct powers of \(k\). The main result of this paper is that \(N(2,1) = N(2,2) = N(2,3) = 129\). In other words, the last number that cannot be written as the sum of one or more distinct squares is 128.

hits.title: Graphs which are vertex-critical with respect to the edge-chromatic class
hits.text: The edge-chromatic number of graph G is denoted by \(\chi '(G)\). A multigraph G is EN-critical (VN-critical) if it is connected, Class 2, and \(\chi '(G-e)<\chi '(G)\) for all edges e in G \((\chi '(G-v)<\chi '(G)\) for all vertices v in G). A multigraph G is EC-critical (VC-critical) if it is connected, Class 2, and G-e is Class 1 for all e in G (G-v is Class 1 for all v in G). For simple graphs EN-critical and EC-critical are equivalent. In this paper a number of interesting results and conjectures are given regarding multigraphs which are EN-critical but not EC- critical, regarding the relationship between VN-critical and VC-critical graphs and the relationship between VC-critical and EC-critical graphs.

hits.title: Problems on Hall \(t\)-chromaticity.
hits.text:
A graph \(G\) with vertex demands is said to satisfy Hall's condition for \(t\) colors, if for each subgraph \(H\) of \(G\), the quantity \(t\alpha (H)\) is equal to the sum of the demands of vertices of \(H\). Here \(\alpha (H)\) stands for the size of a maximum independent set of \(H\).

Hall condition is necessary for the existence of a multicoloring by \(t\) colors satisfying the color demands at each vertex. A Hall \(t\)-chromatic graph is a graph such that the Hall condition is sufficient for any color demands.

The paper provides a construction of a family of graphs that are not Hall \(t\)-chromatic for all \(t\geq 3\) and which yields new conditions in characterization of Hall \(t\)-chromatic graphs.

hits.title: The connected hub number and the connected domination number
hits.text: Summary: The connected hub number \(h_{c}(G)\) of a connected graph \(G\) is the smallest order of a connected subgraph \(H\) of \(G\) such that any two nonadjacent vertices of \(G - H\) are joined in \(G\) by a path with all internal vertices in \(H\). Letting \(\gamma _{c}(G)\) denote the connected domination number of \(G\), it is easy to see that \(h_{c}(G) \leq \gamma_{c}(G) \leq h_{c}(G) + 1\) for every connected graph \(G\). Here we characterize the graphs \(G\) for which \(\gamma_{c}(G) = h_{c}(G) + 1\). Our result contributes to the search for the solution of an extremal problem of \textit{R. E. Newman-Wolfe}, \textit{R. D. Dutton} and \textit{R. C. Brigham} [Congr. Numerantium 67, 67--76 (1988; Zbl 0675.05037)].

hits.title: How to find a defense against an attack, when there is one
hits.text: Summary: An efficient algorithm is described for finding a successful defense against an attack on a set of vertices in a graph, when there is such a defense. The algorithm boils down to finding a maximum matching in a bipartite graph.

hits.title: Theta graphs are Hall \(t\)-chromatic for all \(t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)
hits.text: Summary: It is shown that every graph made up of internally disjoins paths joining two vertices is Hall $t$-chromatic for all non-negative integern $t$.

hits.title: Relaxations of the definition of regular clique assemblies
hits.text: Summary: A regular clique assembly is a regular graph \(G\), with clique number at least 2 such that every maximal clique of \(G\) is maximum and every edge of \(G\) is in exactly one maximum clique of \(G\). This paper is about the consequences of relaxing certain conditions of this definition and the structure of the resulting graphs.

hits.title: Estimates of the choice numbers and the Ohba numbers of some complete multipartite graphs.
hits.text: The Ohba number of a graph \(G\) is defined as the smallest integer \(n\) such that the join \(G\vee K_n\) satisfies \(\operatorname{ch}(G\vee K_n)=\chi (G\vee K_n)\), where \(\operatorname{ch}(G)\) and \(\chi (G)\) are the choice number and chromatic number of \(G\), respectively [\textit{K. Ohba}, J. Graph Theory 40, No. 2, 130--135 (2002; Zbl 1004.05030)]. In this paper, some estimates of the choice numbers and Ohba numbers of the complete multipartite graphs \(K(m,n,1,\dots ,1)\) and \(K(m,n,2,\dots ,2)\) are given for various values of \(m\geq n\geq 1\). For example, for complete \(k\)-partite graphs we have \(\operatorname{ch}(K(m,n,1,\dots ,1))\leq n+k-1\), \(\operatorname{ch}(K(m,2,\dots ,2))\leq 2k-1\) and equality holds for \(m\geq {{2k-2}\choose {k-1}}^{2}\).

hits.title: A mixed Ramsey problem revisited
hits.source: Int. J. Math. Comput. Sci. 16, No. 2, 723-727 (2021).
hits.text: Summary: It is shown that for each integer \(n>1\), \(\{k:\exists\) an edge coloring of \(K_n\) with exactly \(k\) colors appearing in which exactly 2 colors appear on the edges of each \(K_3\) in \(K_n\}=\{g(n),\dots,n-1\}\), a block of consecutive integers in which \(g(n)\in\{\lceil 2\log_5n\rceil\), \(\lceil 2\log_5n\rceil+1\}\). This is a sharpening of a result of \textit{F. R. K. Chung} and \textit{R. L. Graham} [Combinatorica 3, 315--324 (1983; Zbl 0529.05041)].

hits.title: Graphs that accept forced relative self-complementation
hits.text: Summary: A (multi)graph \(G\) with \(2k\) edges and no isolated vertices is \(k\)-good if and only if for each subgraph \(H\) of \(G\) with \(k\) edges and no isolated vertices, the subgraph of \(G\) induced by the \(k\) edges of \(E(G)\setminus E(H)\) is isomorphic to \(H\). We find all \(k\)-good graphs for all \(k= 1,2,\dots\).

hits.title: Yet another species of forbidden-distances chromatic number
hits.text: The upper chromatic number of a metric space \((X,d)\) is the smallest positive integer \(m\) such that for each sequence \(s_1,\dots, s_m> 0\) there is a partition of \(X\) into sets \(X_1,\dots, X_m\) (here allowed to be empty) such that no two points of \(X_i\) are a distance \(s_i\) apart, \(i= 1,\dots, m\). The authors promote the study of another sequence of forbidden-distance chromatic numbers related to the upper chromatic numbers, but seemingly much more tractable: for \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and metric space \((X,d)\), \(B_k(X)\) is the smallest \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) (if any) such that for every set of \(k\) or fewer positive numbers, there is a coloring of \(X\) with \(m\) colors with every distance in the set forbidden for every color.

hits.title: Coloring the edges of \(K_n\) to forbid \(k\)-rainbow graphs
hits.text: Summary: Suppose \(k\) is a positive integer. An edge-colored graph \(G\) is \(k\)-rainbow if and only if no color appears on more than \(k\) edges of \(G\). The notation \(AR_k(G, n)\) denotes the largest number of colors appearing in an edge coloring of \(K_n\) which admits no \(k\)-rainbow copy of \(G\). The graph \(G\) is \(AR_k\)-bounded if and only if the sequence \((AR_k(G,n))_{n>1}\) is bounded. We determine all \(AR_k\)-bounded graphs, for all \(k\in\mathbb{Z}^+\).

hits.title: Existence of multi-Latin squares satisfying a persistent Sudoku condition
hits.text: Summary: Suppose that \(n\), \(k\), and \(d\) are positive integers and \(k\) divides \(n\); say, \(n=mk\). A \textit{multi-latin square} is an  \(n\times n\) array on \(m\) symbols such that each symbol appears exactly \(k\) times in each row and in each column. Such a square is in the subcollection \(\mathrm{ML}_d(n,k)\) if in each \(d\times d\) block of the array -- such a block is the intersection of \(d\) consecutive rows of the array with \(d\) consecutive columns -- none of the \(m\) symbols appears more than once. We show that for \(d>1\), \(\mathrm{ML}_d(n,k)\) multilatin squares exist if and only if \(m\geq d^2+1\), and give a construction for an \(\mathrm{ML}_d(n,k)\) array when this inequality holds.

hits.title: Frobenius problems in integral domains
hits.text: Summary: From the well-known Frobenius problems in the integers and the recent formulation of Frobenius problems in the Gaussian integers [\textit{K. Dutch} et al., Geombinatorics 20, No. 3, 93--109 (2011)] we extract a general format for Frobenius problems in arbitrary rings. Results are given and questions posed about these problems in quadratic extensions of the integers.

hits.title: How does one cut a triangle? With forewords by Philip L. Engel, Paul Erdős, Branko Grünbaum, Peter D. Johnson jun. and Cecil Rousseau
hits.text:
In the second edition of an engagingly written book [see Zbl 0691.52001 , ME 1991h.02126 for the first edition], addressed to bright high school students and undergraduates, whose contributions are very nicely incorporated into the narrative, the author presents problems belonging to discrete and combinatorial geometry. It starts by solving the problem of (1) finding all positive integers \(n\) for which every triangle can be cut into \(n\) triangles similar to each other (all \(n\neq 2, 3, 5\)), and the problem of (2) finding all positive integers \(n\) for which every triangle can be cut into \(n\) triangles congruent to each other (all \(n = k^2\), for some \(k\geq 1\)). It then moves on to provide two proofs for the fact that (3) of any five points in a triangle of unit area there are three that form a triangle of area \(\leq \frac{1}{4}\). 

R. Peng showed in 1989, while a senior high school student, that \(\leq \frac{1}{4}\) can be replaced in (3) with \(\leq (\sqrt{2}-1)^2\), and that this is the best possible constant. With \(S_{\alpha}(F)\) defined as the minimal positive integer \(n\) such that among any \(n\) points located inside or on the boundary of the figure \(F\), there are three points which form a triangle of area at most \(\alpha \cdot |F|\) where \(|F|\) denotes the area of \(F\), the author shows that \(S_{\frac{1}{4}}(F)\) must be 5 or 6 for all convex figures \(F\), and that both 5 and 6 occur (5 whenever \(F\) is a triangle, and 6 when \(F\) is a regular pentagon).

Among the many Erdős conjectures to be found in this book, we mention two: (4) That, among all triangles formed by three of the vertices of any convex pentagon of unit area, one must have an area of at most \(\frac{5-\sqrt{5}}{10}\), and that this bound (attained in the case of the regular pentagon) is best possible; (5) Find the smallest and the largest value of \(\alpha\) such that for every convex figure \(F\), \(S_{\alpha}(F)\) is 5 or 6.

A second part was added to this second edition, on developments since the publication of the first edition (1990). It contains another proof of (1), several results by M. Laczkovicz on cutting triangles, the result of the collaboration of the author with J. H. Conway, regarding the number of unit equilateral triangles it takes to cover an equilateral triangle of side \(n + \varepsilon\) (\(n^2 + 2\) unit equilateral triangles suffice, and it is conjectured that \(n^2 + 1\) do not suffice). Somewhat confusingly, it also contains M. Kahle's improvement of \(\leq \frac{1}{4}\) in (3) to \(\leq \frac{6}{25}\) and his conjecture that the best possible constant in (3) is \(\frac{1}{6}\) (although the matter had been settled by Peng's result, and the conjecture disproved).

However, Kahle's involvement with the problem fits nicely with the overall message of the book, that elementary mathematics fascinates those who have encountered it while they were in high school long after their Olympiad experiences are over. Kahle had encountered (3) on one of his five attendances of the Colorado Mathematical Olympiad (called into life and run for 26 years by the author) in 1988, and provided the improved bound 20 years later -- while a Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford. The fact that Kahle, a two time gold medalist of the Colorado Mathematical Olympiad, had not been admitted to the University of Colorado at Colorado Springs for grade point average reasons speaks eloquently about both the ineptitude of the admission rules and regulations and the irrelevance of the institution of high school mathematics in the United States of America (which is, at best, concerned with questions of the kind ``prove that \(A\) implies \(B\) using the Pythagorean theorem'' (Preface, xxix)), and leaves graduates ``without the foggiest idea of what mathematics is'' (Preface, xxviii), as the latter assigned Kahle a grade of C in geometry.

hits.title: Note on the inverse domination number problem
hits.text: Summary: The problem is to decide on the conjecture that the inverse domination number of a graph with no isolated vertices is necessarily no greater than the vertex independence number. We prove a modest lemma of possible use in this matter, and use it to give a new proof of the known fact that the conjecture holds for claw-free graphs.

hits.title: A problem in graph theory arising from air traffic control
hits.text:
Summary: From one of the approaches to the problem of resectorization in air traffic control comes the following: 



Given a connected finite simple graph \(G= (V,E)\) with weights \(wt: V\to(0,\infty)\), partition \(V\) into two sets \(U\), \(W\) such that \(G[U]\), \(G[W]\) are connected and 

\[
\left|\sum_{u\in U} wt(u)- \sum_{w\in W} wt(w)\right|
\]
 
is minimized. We propose an obvious class of heuristic algorithms for approximately solving the problem: find a spanning tree in \(G\) and solve the problem for the tree, with the same weights. Much experimentation and analysis remains to be done.

hits.text: Summary: An inequality for double integrals involving two measurable non-negative functions on a probability space is proved, using a special case of Hölder's inequality.

hits.title: Fractional inverse and inverse fractional domination.
hits.text: Summary: We examine the inverse domination number of a graph, as well as two reasonable candidates for the fractional analogue of this parameter. We also examine the relations among these and other graph parameters. In particular, we show that both proposed fractional analogues of the inverse domination number are no greater than the fractional independence number. These results establish the fractional analogue of a well-known conjecture about the inverse domination and vertex independence numbers of a graph.

hits.title: Coloring Euclidean spaces so that all translates of a given set are rainbow
hits.text: Summary: If \(T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(|T|=3\), and \(T\) is contained in no line, then \(\mathbb{R}^n\) can be ``slab''-colored with 3 colors so that every translate of \(T\) in \(R^n\) is ``rainbow'', meaning that no two of the three elements of \(T\) bear the same color. If \(T\) is contained in a line, then 4 colors may be required, but never more than 4. If \(|T|=k>3\), similar results hold, but more questions remain open than in the case \(k=3\).

hits.title: A note on stable matchings
hits.source: Int. J. Math. Comput. Sci. 8, No. 2, 35-36 (2013).
hits.text:
Summary: The Gale-Shapley theorem, sometimes called the stable marriage theorem, asserts that there is a stable matching in every finite locally ordered bipartite graph. We show that this statement characterizes
bipartite graphs, among finite simple graphs.

hits.title: Sharpening the Faudree-Knisley theorem on \((2,r)\)-regularity
hits.text:
A simple graph \(G\) is \((2,r)\)-regular if the union of the neighborhoods of any two non-adjacent vertices has precisely \(r\) vertices and \(G\) is not complete. It is shown that if \(G\) is a graph of order \(n \geq r^2\) that is \((2,r)\)-regular, then \(G\) is of the form \(K_s + (mK_p)\) for some \(m \geq 2\), \(p \geq 1\) and \(s \geq 0\) satisfying \(s + 2(p - 1) = r\). It is also shown that \(n \geq r^2/16\) is not sufficiently large for this result.

This improves a result of \textit{R. Faudree} and \textit{D. Knisley} [Congr. Numerantium 121, 105--108 (1996; Zbl 0896.05052)] both in complexity of proof and improvement on bounds for \(n\).

hits.title: Reverse class critical multigraphs
hits.text:
Let be \(G=G(V,E)\) a loopless multigraph with the maximum degree \(\Delta\) (G) and the chromatic index \(\chi'(G).\) If \(\Delta(G)=\chi'(G)\), then G is said to be Class 1, and otherwise G is Class 2. In this note are considered multigraphs with the property that upon the removal of any vertex the chromatic class rises. And a multigraph is called reverse class critical (exactly vertex reverse class critical or VRC-critical multigraph) if G is Class 1 but \(G\setminus v\) is Class 2 for each \(v\in V(G).\) 


It is well-known that \(K_{2p}\) is Class 1 and it is shown that also \(K_{2p}^{(r)}\) is Class 1 for all \(r\geq 1\) (let \(K_ n^{(r)}\) denote the graph obtained from \(K_ n\) by replicating each edge r times). By using this result those VRC-critical multigraphs are characterized which have at least two vertices of degree r(n-1) [Theorem 3]. And by applying Theorem 3 there follows a characterization of VRC- critical simple graphs G if holds that \(| V(G)|\) is even. In this case a lower bound for \(| E(G)|\) is deduced in Theorem 4.

hits.title: On graphs with no proper perfect dominating set
hits.text: Summary: A set of vertices in a graph is perfect dominating if every vertex outside the set is adjacent to exactly one vertex in the set, and is neighborhood connected if the subgraph induced by its open neighborhood is connected. In any graph the full set of vertices is perfect dominating, and in every connected graph the full set of vertices is neighborhood connected. It is shown that (i) in a connected graph, if the only neighborhood connected perfect dominating set is the full set of vertices, then the full set of vertices is also the only perfect dominating set, (ii) if \(r\geq 3 \) and \(n_1, \ldots , n_r \geq 2 \), then in \(K_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{r}}\) the only perfect dominating set is the full set of vertices and (iii) estimates are derived of how many edges can be removed from or added to \(K_{n_{1},\ldots, n_{r}}\) while preserving the property described in (ii).
