hits.title: Three-monotone interpolation
hits.text: Inspired by the classical results on \(k\)-monotone interpolability for \(k = 1\) and \(k = 2\) due to \textit{P. Erdős} and \textit{G. Szekeres} from [Compos. Math. 2, 463--470 (1935; JFM 61.0651.04)], the authors investigate the \(3\)-monotone interpolability, showing for instance that it is very nonlocal, by providing an arbitrarily large and finite two-dimensional set \(P\) which is not \(3\)-monotone interpolable, but all its proper subsets are. Moreover, a Ramsey-type result is also proven, namely that for every positive integer \(n\) there exists another positive integer \(N\) such that every \(N\)-point with distinct \(x\)-coordinates contains an \(n\)-point that is \(3\)-monotone interpolable or its vertical mirror reflection has this property. An example where this semidefinite program has only doubly exponentially large feasible solutions and thus known algorithms cannot solve it in polynomial time is provided, being arguably the first of its kind in polynomial optimization in the literature.

hits.title: Peeling potatoes near-optimally in near-linear time
hits.text: Summary: We consider the following geometric optimization problem: find a convex polygon of maximum area contained in a given simple polygon \(P\) with \(n\) vertices. We give a randomized near-linear-time \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm for this problem: in \(O(n(\log^2n+(1/\varepsilon^3)\log n+1/\varepsilon^4))\) time we find a convex polygon contained in \(P\) that, with probability at least \(2/3\), has area at least \((1-\varepsilon)\) times the area of an optimal solution. We also obtain similar results for the variant of computing a convex polygon inside \(P\) with maximum perimeter. To achieve these results we provide new results in geometric probability. The first result is a bound relating the area of the largest convex body inside \(P\) to the probability that two points chosen uniformly at random inside \(P\) are mutually visible. The second result is a bound on the expected value of the difference between the perimeter of any planar convex body \(K\) and the perimeter of the convex hull of a uniform random sample inside \(K\).

Summary: Motivated by recent papers of \textit{D. Eppstein} [in: Proceedings of the 23rd annual symposium on computational geometry, SoCG '07. New York, NY: ACM Press. 92--101 (2007; Zbl 1221.05292)], \textit{Z. Abel} et al. [Graphs Comb. 27, No. 1, 47--60 (2011; Zbl 1236.52013)], \textit{J. Bárat} et al. [``Empty pentagons in point sets with collinearities'', SIAM J. Discrete Math. 29, No. 1, 198--209 (2015; \url{doi:10.1137/130950422})], and by a question of Wood, we investigate properties of planar point sets with no 5-hole (no empty convex pentagon). We answer a question of Wood by showing that the visibility graph of a finite point set with no 5-hole may contain a clique of arbitrary size. This is in contrast with the previous examples of sets with no 5-hole, including the example of the (finite) square lattice. In our construction we use several equivalent local characterizations of (locally) finite planar point sets with no 5-hole which may be of independent interest. Our construction relies on a construction scheme which allows to derive new, non-trivial examples of sets with no 5-hole.

hits.title: On the geometric Ramsey number of outerplanar graphs
hits.text:
The geometric Ramsey number \(n\) of a graph is the smallest integer where every complete geometric graph on \(n\) vertices with edges arbitarily colored by two colors contains a monochromatic non-crossing copy of the original graph.

For any integer \(n\), a ladder graph on \(2n\) vertices is the graph composed of two paths \((u_i)_{i=1}^n\) and \((v_i)_{i=1}^n\) together with the set of edges \(\{u_iv_i: i =1,\ldots,n\}\).

From the authors' summary:``We prove polynomial upper bounds of geometric Ramsey numbers of pathwidth-2 outerplanar triangulations in both convex and general cases. We also prove that the geometric Ramsey numbers of the ladder graph on \(2n\) vertices are bounded by \(O(n^3)\) and \(O(n^{10})\), in the convex and general case, respectively. We then apply similar methods to prove an \(n^{O(\log(n))}\) upper bound on the Ramsey number of a path with \(n\) ordered vertices''.

hits.title: Covering lattice points by subspaces and counting point-hyperplane incidences
hits.source: Aronov, Boris (ed.) et al., 33rd international symposium on computational geometry. SoCG 2017, Brisbane, Australia, July 4--7, 2017. Proceedings. Wadern: Schloss Dagstuhl -- Leibniz Zentrum für Informatik. LIPIcs -- Leibniz Int. Proc. Inform. 77, Article 12, 16 p. (2017).
hits.text:
Summary: Let \(d\) and \(k\) be integers with \(1\leq k\leq d-1\). Let \(\Lambda\) be a \(d\)-dimensional lattice and let \(K\) be a \(d\)-dimensional compact convex body symmetric about the origin. We provide estimates for the minimum number of \(k\)-dimensional linear subspaces needed to cover all points in \(\Lambda\cap K\). In particular, our results imply that the minimum number of \(k\)-dimensional linear subspaces needed to cover the \(d\)-dimensional \(n\times\cdots\times n\) grid is at least \(\Omega(n^{(d(d-k)/(d-1)-\varepsilon})\) and at most \(O(n^{d(d-k)/(d-1)})\), where \(\varepsilon>0\) is an arbitrarily small constant. This nearly settles a problem mentioned in the book of \textit{P. Brass} et al. [Research problems in discrete geometry. New York, NY: Springer (2005; Zbl 1086.52001)]. We also find tight bounds for the minimum number of \(k\)-dimensional affine subspaces needed to cover \(\Lambda\cap K\).

We use these new results to improve the best known lower bound for the maximum number of point-hyperplane incidences by \textit{P. Brass} and \textit{Knauer} [Comput. Geom. 25, No. 1--2, 13--20 (2003; Zbl 1022.65021)]. For \(d\geq 3\) and \(\varepsilon\in (0,1)\), we show that there is an integer \(r=r(d,\varepsilon)\) such that for all positive integers \(n,m\) the following statement is true. There is a set of \(n\) points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) and an arrangement of \(m\) hyperplanes in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with no \(K_{r,r}\) in their incidence graph and with at least \(\Omega((mn)^{1-(2d+3)/((d+2)(d+3))-\varepsilon})\) incidences if \(d\) is odd and \(\Omega((mn)^{1-(2d^2+d-2)/((d+2)(d^2+2d-2))-\varepsilon})\) incidences if \(d\) is even.

hits.title: A probabilistic approach to the problem of the defects of admissible sets in a lattice
hits.source: Math. Notes 68, No. 6, 770-774 (2000); translation from Mat. Zametki 68, No. 6, 910-916 (2000).
hits.text:
Let \(L\) be a nondegenerate homogeneous lattice in \(\mathbb R^n\) containing the integer lattice \(\mathbb Z^n\) as a sublattice. The defect \(d(L)\) of \(E\) in \(L\) is defined as the smallest number of vectors to be deleted from the frame \(E=\{o,e_1,\dots,e_n\}\) made up of the origin and the unit coordinate vectors such that the remaining system be complementable to a basis of \(L\). Consider an arbitrary sequence of sets \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2,\dots\) such that, for each \(n\in \mathbb N\), \(\Omega_n\) contains \(\pm E\) and is contained in the cube \([-1,1]^n\); moreover, the intersection of \(\Omega_n\) with each of the \(k\)-dimensional coordinate planes is supposed to be a copy of \(\Omega_k\). A set \(\Omega_n\) is called admissible in \(L\) if its intersection with \(L\) is \(\pm E\). Given any such set, one may speak of \(d(L)\) as of the defect of the admissible set \(\Omega_n\) in \(L\), and denote this by \(d(\Omega_n,L)\). There are various classes of popular examples, e.g. the hyperbolic crosses and the Minkowski set \({\mathcal B}_{n,\alpha}: |x_1|^\alpha+\cdots+|x_n|^\alpha\leq 1\) \((\alpha>0)\).


Now let \(d(\Omega_n)=\max_L d(\Omega_n,L)\) and \(d^*(\Omega_n)=\max_{L'}d(\Omega_n,L')\), where the first maximum is taken over all lattices of the kind described, and the second maximum is taken over the restricted class of lattices which are obtained from \(\mathbb Z^n\) by adjoining a single (rational) point. The author presents some asymptotic bounds for these quantities (partly involving octahedra \({\mathcal B}_{n,1}\) and balls \({\mathcal B}_{n,2}\)) which can be derived from his earlier papers [Mat. Sb., Nov. Ser. 189, No. 6, 117--141 (1998; Zbl 0926.52019); English transl. in Sb. Math. 189, 931--954 (1998); see also \textit{N. G. Moshchevitin}, Mat. Zametki 58, 558--568 (1995; Zbl 0855.52005) and the author, Grazer Math. Ber. 338, 31--62 (1999; Zbl 0973.11068)]. 


The main result here is concerned with lower estimates of \(d^*(\Omega_n)\) for certain subsequences of dimensions. In contrast to the methods used in the papers mentioned, the present proof is of a probabilistic nature.

Having in mind the classical Erdös-Hadwiger Problem of determining the chromatic numbers of the Euclidean spaces, the author studies the chromatic numbers of the Banach space \(\mathbb R^d\) endowed with the \(l_q\)-metric. We recall that the chromatic number \(\chi(X,d)\) of a metric space \((X,d)\) is the smallest number of colors necessary for coloring the points of \(X\) so that no points on the distance 1 have the same color.

Completing the existing results on the chromatic numbers of finite-dimensional Banach spaces, the author proves two lower bounds: one of them is \(\chi(\mathbb R^d,l_1)\geq (1.365...+o(1))^d\). The other says that for every rational number \(q\geq 1\) we get \(\chi(\mathbb Q^d,l_q)\geq(1+\varepsilon+o(1))^d\) for some \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon(q)>0\).

Summary: This paper explores the application of a new algebraic method of colour exchanges to the edge colouring of simple graphs. Vizing's theorem states that the edge colouring of a simple graph \(G\) requires either \(\Delta\) or \(\Delta+1\) colours, where \(\Delta\) is the maximum vertex degree of \(G\). Holyer proved that it is \(NP\)-complete to decide whether \(G\) is \(\Delta\)-edge colourable even for cubic graphs.


 By introducing the concept of complex coloured edges, we show that the colour-exchange operation of complex colours follows the same multiplication rules as quaternion. An initially \(\Delta\)-edge-coloured graph \(G\) allows variable-coloured edges, which can be eliminated by colour exchanges in a manner similar to variable eliminations in solving systems of linear equations. The problem is solved if all variables are eliminated and a properly \(\Delta\)-edge-coloured graph is reached.


 For \(\Delta\)-regular uniform random graphs, we prove that our algorithm returns a proper \(\Delta\)-edge colouring with a probability of \(1-1/n\) in \(O(n^3_0\Delta^4n^4)\) time if \(G\) is \(\Delta\)-edge colourable. Otherwise, the algorithm halts in polynomial time and signals the impossibility of a solution, meaning that the chromatic index of \(G\) probably equals \(\Delta+1\).

hits.title: Characteristics of the enhanced power coprime graphs of some finite groups
hits.text: Summary: The graphs of groups is a powerful tool for studying finite groups as it visually represents their structures and relationships. In general, introducing new graphs of groups leads to discoveries about the graphs' characteristics, offering significant insights into its structure, connectivity, and spectral aspects. This paper investigates various characteristics of a newly introduced graph called the enhanced power coprime graph of some finite groups. The enhanced power coprime graph of a finite group, \(G\) is defined as a graph with elements of \(G\) as vertices, where two distinct vertices \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent if they generate a proper cyclic subgroup of \(G\) and \(\gcd(|x|, |y|) = 1\). First, we establish the general presentations of the enhanced power coprime graph for all semi-dihedral groups of order \(2^n\) and prime power cases of dihedral and generalized quaternion groups. These presentations facilitate the determination of various characteristics, including vertex degrees, clique numbers, chromatic numbers, independence numbers, domination numbers, girth, diameter, graph classification, and the Laplacian spectrum. The results reveal that the enhanced power coprime graphs of the mentioned groups are connected, planar, and perfect, with consistent characteristics for those with similar presentations. These findings have applications in computational group theory, network analysis, and coding theory, using graph characteristics to explore group structures.

hits.title: Endotrivial modules for the quaternion group and iterated Jokers in chromatic homotopy theory
hits.text: Summary: The algebraic Joker module was originally described in the 1970s by Adams and Priddy and is a $5$-dimensional module over the subHopf algebra $\mathcal{A}(1)$ of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. It is a self-dual endotrivial module, i.e., an invertible object in the stable module category of $\mathcal{A}(1)$. Recently it has been shown that no analogues exist for $\mathcal{A}(n)$ with $n>1$. Using iterated doubling this also gives an iterated double which is an $\mathcal{A}(n)$-module but not stably invertible. In previous work the author showed that for $n=1,2,3$ these iterated doubles were realisable as cohomology of CW spectra, but no such realisation existed for $n>3$. The main point of the paper is to show that in the height $2$ chromatic context, the Morava $K$-theory of double Jokers realise an exceptional endotrivial module over the quaternion group of order $8$ that only exists over a field of characteristic $2$ containing a primitive cube root of unity. This has connections with certain Massey products in the cohomology of the quaternion group.

hits.text:
Let \(f : \widehat{{\mathbb C}} \to \widehat{{\mathbb C}}\) be a 3-fold branched covering with branch points \(\{ 0,1,\infty, \lambda \}\), where \(\lambda\) is a variable point in \(\widehat{{\mathbb C}}-\{ 0,1,\infty \}\). Two such coverings \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are said to be equivalent if there exist an (analytic) isomorphism \(g : \widehat{{\mathbb C}} \to \widehat{{\mathbb C}}\) such that \(f_1=f_2\circ g\). The set of equivalence classes, which is called an Hurwitz space, inherits a topology and a complex structure. A branched covering is said to be irreducible if no intermediate coverings exist. A branch point is said to be simple if the inverse image by \(f\) contains only one ramification point and the local degree of \(f\) at the ramification point is two. In this paper the author gives an example of 1-dimensional Hurwitz space of irreducible branched coverings of degree three with four simple branch points by using the monodromy representation \(\omega : \pi_1(\widehat{{\mathbb C}}-\{0,1, \infty, \lambda \}, i) \to \Sigma_3\), where \(\Sigma\) denotes the symmetric group on three letters, and by ''coloring the strings''. Also the author describes the Hurwitz space in relation to the Belyi curve in the case that the monodromy group is the dihedral group of order \(2p\), where \(p\) is prime.

hits.title: On set-systems having large chromatic number and not containing prescribed subsystems
hits.source: Infinite finite Sets, Colloq. Honour Paul Erdős, Keszthely 1973, Colloq. Math. Soc. János Bolyai 10, 425-513 (1975).
hits.text:
This lengthy paper is devoted to a variety of problems concerning the chromatic number of set systems. A ``set system'' is defined to be a family of \(S\) of sets each of at least two elements. The ``chromatic number'' of \(S\) is the smallest cardinal \(\kappa\) for which there is a partition of length \(\kappa\) of \(\cup S\), \(\cup S= \cup \{P_\nu; \nu < \kappa \}\), such that \(A \not\subseteq P_\nu\) whenever \(A \in S\), \(\nu < \kappa\). The family \(S\) is said to be an \((n,i)\)-system if it is a family of \(n\)-tuples every two of which have at most \(i\) elements in common. 

 In an earlier paper [Cambridge Summer School Math. Logic, Cambridge 1971, Lecture Notes Math. 337, 531--538 (1973; Zbl 0289.04002)], \textit{P. Erdős}, \textit{A. Hajnal} and \textit{B. Rothchild} have shown that if \(1 \leq i \leq n< \omega \leq \kappa\) then there is an \((n,i)\)-system with chromatic number \(>\kappa\), and that the cardinality of such a system must be large. One of the aims of the present paper is to determine just how large. The following are proved: (a) Assume \(mi+2 \leq n< \aleph_0\). Let \(S\) be a system of \(n\)-tuples with \(|S| = \aleph_{\alpha +m}\) such that every \(\aleph_{\alpha +1}\)-size subset of \(S\) has at most \(i\) elements in its intersection. Then \(S\) has chromatic number at most \(\aleph_\alpha\). (b) Assume \(2 \leq n<mi+2< \aleph_0\) and that G.C.H. holds. Then there is an \((n,i)\)-system of cardinality \(\aleph_{\alpha +m}\) and chromatic number \(>\aleph_\alpha\). 

The G.C.H. is needed in (b), for it is shown that if \(MA_\kappa\) holds then every (3,1)-system of cardinality \(\kappa\) has chromatic number at \(\{u \in P |u \sim x, u \sim y, u \sim z \}\). Bose has proved that \(|tr(x,y,z)| =q+1\). The triple \((x,y,z)\), \(x \not\sim\), \(y \not\sim z\), \(z \not\sim x\), is said to be regular provided each point collinear with at least three points of \(tr(x,y,z)\) is actually collinear with all points of \(tr(x,y,z)\). If for a point \(x\) each triple \((x,y,z)\), with \(x \not\sim y\), \(y \not\sim z\), \(z \not\sim x\), is regular, \(x\) is said to be regular. 

The following theorems are proved: 

a) If the 4-gonal configuration \(S\) with parameters \(r=q^2+1\) and \(k=q+1\), where \(q\) is even and \(q>2\), possesses a regular point, then \(S\) is isomorphic to a 4-gonal configuration \(T(0)\) (i.e. a 4-gonal configuration arising from an ovoid 0 of \(\mathrm{PG}(3,q)\)) of \textit{J. Tits}. 

b) If each point of the 4-gonal configuration \(S\) with parameters \(r=q^2+1\) and \(k=q+1\) \((q>2)\) is regular, then \(S\) is isomorphic to the 4-gonal configuration \(Q(5,q)\) arising from a non-singular hyperquadric \(Q\) of index 2 of \(\mathrm{PG}(5,q)\). 

c) Suppose that the 4-gonal configuration \(S=(P,B,I)\), with parameters \(r=q^2+1\) and \(k=q+1\) \((q>1)\), has a 4-gonal subconfiguration \(S' =(P' ,B' ,I)\), with parameters \(k' = r' =k\), for which the following condition is satisfied: if \(x,y,z \in P'\) with \(x \not\sim y\), \(y \not\sim z\), \(z \not\sim x\), then the triple \((x,y,z)\) is regular and moreover \(sp(x,y,z) \subset P'\). Then we have (i) \(S\) has an involution with fixes \(P'\) pointwise (ii) \(S'\) is isomorphic to the 4-gonal configuration \(Q(4,q)\) arising from a non-singular hyperquadric in \(\mathrm{PG}(4,q)\). 


Remark: Recently the author has proved a) for \(q\) odd.

hits.title: Sharp bounds for the number of 3-independent partitions and the chromaticity of bipartite graphs
hits.text: Summary: Given a graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\geq 1\), let \(\alpha (G,k)\) denote the number of \(k\)-independent partitions of \(G\). Let \({\mathcal K}^{-s}(p,q)\) (resp., \({\mathcal K}_2^{-s}(p,q))\) denote the family of connected (resp., 2-connected) graphs which are obtained from the complete bipartite graph \(K_{p,q}\) by deleting a set of \(s\) edges, where \(p\geq q\geq 2\). This paper first gives a sharp upper bound for \(\alpha(G,3)\), where \(G\in{\mathcal K}^{-s}(p,q)\) and \(0\leq s\leq(p-1)(q-1)\) (resp., \(G\in{\mathcal K}_2^{-s}(p,q)\) and \(0\leq s\leq p+q-4)\). These bounds are then used to show that if \(G\in{\mathcal K}^{-s}(p,q)\) (resp., \(G \in {\mathcal K}_2^{-s}(p,q))\), then the chromatic equivalence class of \(G\) is a subset of the union of the sets \({\mathcal K}^{-s_i} (p+i,q-i)\) where \(\max\{-{s \over q-1},-{p-q \over 2}\}\leq i\leq {s\over p-1}\) and \(s_i=s-i(p-q+i)\) (resp., a subset of \({\mathcal K}_2^{-s}(p,q)\), where either \(0\leq s\leq q-1\), or \(s\leq 2q-3\) and \(p\geq q+4)\). By applying these results, we show finally that any 2-connected graph obtained from \(K_{p,q}\) by deleting a set of edges that forms a matching of size at most \(q-1\) or that induces a star is chromatically unique.

hits.title: An algebraic criterion for a graph to be four-colourable
hits.source: Rentería, Carlos (ed.) et al., International seminar on algebra and its applications. Proceedings, Mexico City, Mexico, January 20--26, 1991. Mexico City: Sociedad Matemática Mexicana. Aportaciones Mat., Notas Invest. 6, 3-27 (1992).
hits.text:
Let \(X= (X_0, X_1)\) be any finite graph with vertex set \(X_0= \{1,\dots, n\}\) and edge set \(X_1\). A proper \(q\)-colouring of \(X\) is a map \(c: X_0\to G\) from \(X_0\) to some fixed set \(G\) of cardinality \(q\), such that \(c(i)\neq c(j)\) whenever \(\{i, j\}\) is an edge in \(X\). The graph \(X\) is said to be \(q\)-colourable if it admits a proper \(q\)-colouring. The set of colours \(G\) is usually irrelevant. However, choosing \(G\) to be an abelian group enables us to establish algebraic criteria for \(X\) to be \(q\)-colourable. We consider here, in some detail, the case \(q= 4\) and \(G= C_2\times C_2\), where \(C_2\) denotes the multiplicative group \(\{+ 1,- 1\}\). The corresponding algebraic criterion takes then the following form. Let \(A_{2n}\) be the quotient ring 
\[
A_{2n}= \mathbb{Q}[x_1,\dots, x_n, y_1,\dots, y_n]/(x^2_i- 1, y^2_i- 1\mid i= 1,\dots, n).
\]
 To the graph \(X\) we associate an element \(\delta_X\in A_{2n}\) as follows: 
\[
\delta_X= \prod_{\{i, j\}\in X_1} (3- x_i x_j- y_i y_j- x_i x_j y_i y_j).
\]
 This element will be shown to have the following basic properties: (1) \(X\) is 4-colourable if and only if \(\delta_X\neq 0\). (2) The constant term of \(\delta_X\) equals \(4^{|X_1|- |X_0|}\cdot P_X(4)\), where \(P_X(4)\) denotes the number of proper 4-colourings of \(X\).


The result above is proved in Section 3, after some preliminary material given in Section 2. By property (2) above, every way of extracting the constant term of \(\delta_X\) will automatically yield a formula for \(P_X(4)\). This makes the content of both Section 4 and Section 5: in each one, we compute the constant term of \(\delta_X\) in a certain way, thereby obtaining formulas for \(P_X(4)\).


The computation in Section 4 enables us to recover (for \(q= 4\)) a well-known expression for the chromatic polynomial \(P_X(q)\), due to \textit{H. Whitney} [Bull. Am. Math. Soc. 38, 572-579 (1932; Zbl 0005.14602)].


In Section 5, the resulting formula for \(P_X(4)\) seems to be new in its generality. In fact, our formula generalizes to arbitrary simple graphs a formula for planar graphs that \textit{N. L. Biggs} obtained in the context of interaction models in statistical mechanics [Interaction models (1977; Zbl 0375.05039)]. His formula is a partition function over the dual graph of the planar graph \(X\); our generalization may be expressed in a similar way, but involves hypergraphs.


The last section is devoted to examples. We start by defining a Laurent polynomial \(\Gamma_X(t)\) attached to the graph \(X\), which is closely related to \(\delta_X\). Then, we compute \(\delta_X\) and \(\Gamma_X(t)\) for trees, for polygons, and for certain triangulations of the plane.


The algebraic criterion involving an arbitrary abelian group \(G\) will be considered in a subsequent paper. For other reformulations of 4-colouring problems, see [\textit{T. L. Saaty} and \textit{P. C. Kainen}, The four-colour problem. Assaults and conguest (1977; Zbl 0463.05041)].

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0845.00036].

hits.title: Existence of nonarithmetic monodromy groups
hits.text: Picard considered in 1885 subgroups \(\Gamma\) (\(\Lambda)\) in the group PU(2,1) generated by monodromies and depending on four rational parameters \(\Lambda =(\lambda_ 1,\lambda_ 2,\lambda_ 3,\lambda_ 4)\), \(0<\lambda_ i<1\), \(\lambda_ i+\lambda_ j\geq 1\), \(2- \sum_{j\neq i}\lambda_ j\geq 0,\quad 1\leq i<j\leq 4.\) He showed that \(\Gamma\) (\(\Lambda)\) acts discretely in a complex ball for a finite number of collections \(\lambda\) and, for these actions, there exists a finite fundamental polyhedron bounded by three-dimensional faces. However, as it was recently cleared up, Picard's proof (but not the construction!) contains essential gaps. In the present article, all is done for Picard's method of the construction of discrete lattices in a complex ball to become strict. Besides, it has been announced that four collections \(\Lambda\) lead to nonarithmetic lattices in the complex ball. We mention such an interesting result, as well: for all \(\Lambda \in {\mathbb{Q}}^ 4\), such a complex surface S(\(\Lambda)\) exists that \(\pi^ 1(S(\Lambda))\) is a subgroup of finite index in \(\Gamma\) (\(\Lambda)\).

hits.title: Countable Butler groups and vector spaces with four distinguished subspaces
hits.text:
If K is a field, \(K_ n\) denotes the category of K-vector spaces with n distinguished subspaces. It is known that for every countable \({\mathbb{Q}}\)- vector space there are four subspaces such that the set of all endomorphisms leaving invariant these subspaces equals a prescribed \({\mathbb{Q}}\)-algebra, compare \textit{R. Göbel}, \textit{W. May} [J. Pure Appl. Algebra 65, 29-43 (1990; Zbl 0716.16015)] and references given there. Using this realization it is shown that for every countable ring R with \(R^+\) a Butler group there exists a countable rank Butler group B with End \(B\simeq R\), if \(R^+\) is p-reduced for at least four primes. Moreover one can obtain a rigid family \(B_{\alpha}\) \((\alpha <2^{\aleph_ 0})\) of Butler groups, where End \(B_{\alpha}\) is isomorphic to R. The isomorphism can be viewed as a topological isomorphism with respect to natural topologies on R and End \(B_{\alpha}.\) 


Finally the well known correspondence between finite rank Butler groups and finite dimensional vector spaces with distinguished subspaces is generalized to the countable rank case. Because of the wild behaviour of \({\mathbb{Q}}_ 4\) for countable dimension it turns out that Butler groups of countable rank arising from four incomparable types behave ``wild'' as well.

Homotopy groups of certain highly connected manifolds via loop space homology
hits.text: Let \(n\geq 2\) and \(d\) be positive integers such that \(d\leq 3n-2\). In this paper the authors study the homotopy types of \((n-1)\)-connected \(d\)-dimensional closed manifolds. In particular, when \(\dim H^*(M;\mathbb{Q})>4\) they show that the \(p\)-local homotopy groups of \(M\) can be determined by the dimension of the space of indecomposable elements in the cohomology ring \(H^*(M;\mathbb{Q})\) and prove that these \(p\)-local homotopy groups can be expressed as the finite \(p\)-local homotopy groups of spheres. Their proof is based on a careful analysis of the loop homology \(H_*(\Omega M;\mathbb{Q})\).

hits.title: Classifying spaces for branched coverings
hits.text: This paper deals with branched coverings in the category of (PL) manifolds. By associating to a fixed manifold \(M\) the set \(B_k(M)\) of concordance classes of \(k\)-fold branched coverings of \(M\), one gets a contravariant functor from the category of PL manifolds to the category of sets. The author constructs a classifying space \(B_k\) for this functor, by carefully fitting together the classifying spaces \(BO(2)\), representing the branching set (which has codimension 2 in \(M)\), and \(BS_k\) (where \(S_k\) denotes the symmetric group on \(k\) letters), representing the \(k\)-fold covering associated with a branched covering. For certain applications this explicit construction of \(B_k\) has the advantage over the classifying space deduced using Brown's Representability Theorem, that not only every concordance class of branched coverings over \(M\), but every single branched covering over \(M\), can be realized as a pullback of the universal \(k\)-fold branched covering along a map \(M\to B_k\). Classifying certain classes of branched coverings defined by putting restrictions on the type of branching that can occur are also constructed. The author begins a study of the geometry of these classifying spaces by calculating for \(B_k\) the rational homotopy type, which turns out to be a bouquet of Eilenberg-MacLane spaces of type \((\mathbb Q,4)\). Finally the homotopy groups are interpreted geometrically as concordance classes of branched coverings over spheres.

hits.title: The level of orders of integers in algebraic number fields
hits.text: Die Stufe \(s(R)\) eines Ringes \(R\) mit \(1\) ist die minimale Anzahl \(s\), derart daß sich \(-1\) als Summe von \(s\) Quadraten aus \(R\) darstellen läßt; ist eine solche Darstellung unmöglich, so wird \(s(R) = \infty\) gesetzt. Die Stufe eines algebraischen Zahlkörpers ist, sofern endlich, \( =1,2\) oder \(4\). In der Note wird gezeigt, daß in total-imaginären Zahlkörpern mit Maximalordnung \(M\) gilt: \(s(M)\le 4\); für eine beliebige Ordnung ist jedenfalls \(s(R)\le 8\), in abelschen Körpern genauer \(\le 4\). In imaginär-quadratischen Zahlkörpern wird die Stufe für beliebige Ordnungen ausgerechnet. In einem Zusatz wird ein Satz von M. Kneser mit Beweisskizze angegeben, der folgendes besagt: In beliebigen total-imaginären Zahlkörpern ist \(s(R)\le 4\), und es gilt \(s(R)\le 3\), sofern \(s(R\otimes \mathbb Q) <4\) und \(s(R\otimes\mathbb Z_2) <4\).

hits.title: On the torsion of rational elliptic curves over quartic fields
hits.text: For an elliptic curve \(E\) rational over \(\mathbb Q\) and a number field \(K\), let \(E(K)_{\mathrm{tors}}\) be the torsion group of \(K\)-rational points of \(E\). It is important to determine all possible group structures of \(E(K)_{\mathrm{tors}}\), where \(E\) and \(K\) run all over elliptic curves rational over \(\mathbb Q\) and number fields of degree \(d\) respectively. Let \(\Phi_{\mathbb Q}(d)\) be the set of these group structures. The set \(\Phi_{\mathbb Q}(d)\) is determined for \(d\leq 4\). To obtain further information, the authors consider three subsets \(\Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\infty(d)\), \(\Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\star(d)\) and \(\Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\star(d,G)\) defined as follows: Let \(H\in\Phi_{\mathbb Q}(d)\). Then \(H\in \Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\infty(d)\) if \(H\) appears infinitely often for elliptic curves defined over \(\mathbb Q\), base extended to a degree \(d\) number field; \(H\in \Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\star(d)\) if \(H\) occurs infinitely often for elliptic curves defined over a degree \(d\) number field; \(H\in\Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\star(d,G)\) if \(H\in\Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\star(d)\) and \(E({\mathbb Q})_{\mathrm{tors}}\simeq G\) and \(E(K)_{\mathrm{tors}}\simeq H\), for an elliptic curve \(E/\mathbb Q\) and a number field \(K\) of degree \(d\). In this article, the authors determine these subsets in the case that \(d=4\). Let \(C_n\) denote the cyclic group of order \(n\). They show that the set \(\Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\star(4)\) consists of the groups \(C_n~ (n=1,\dots,10,12,13,15,16,20,24)\), \(C_2\times C_{2m}~ (m=1,\dots,6,8)\), \(C_3\times C_{3m},~C_4\times C_{4m}~ (m=1,2)\),~\(C_5\times C_5\) and \(C_6\times C_6\), and that \(\Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\infty(4)=\Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\star(4)\setminus \{C_{15}\}\). The set \(\Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\star(4,G)\) is completely determined for each \(G\in \Phi_{\mathbb Q}(1)\). They give some examples to describe an algorithm to compute the quartic fields where the torsion grows for a given elliptic curve rational over \(\mathbb Q\). Further they determine, for many elliptic curves \(E/\mathbb Q\) with \(G_E=E(\mathbb Q)_{\mathrm{tors}}\), all torsion groups \(H_j=E(K_j)_{\mathrm{tors}}\in \Phi_{\mathbb Q}^\star(4,G)\setminus \{G_E\} (j=1,\cdots m_E)\), where \(K_j\) are number fields (non-isomorphic pairwise) of degree \(2\) or \(4\) and \(K_j\) is the smallest number field in the sense that \(H_j\neq E(K')_{\mathrm{tors}}\) for any subfield \(K'\) of \(K_j\). Let \(h_{\mathbb Q}(4)\) be the supremum of the numbers \(m_E\), where \(E\) runs all over non-isomorphic elliptic curves rational over \(\mathbb Q\). The authors show that \(h_{\mathbb Q}(4)\geq 9\). It is a remaining problem to determine \(h_{\mathbb Q}(4)\).

hits.title: Secondary Brown-Kervaire quadratic forms and \(\pi\)-manifolds
hits.text: This paper gives a complete classification of \((n-2)\)-connected \(2n\)-dimensional \(\pi\) manifolds up to homeomorphism and homotopy equivalence when \(n \geq 4\) and \(n+2 \neq 2^i\). In particular, homotopy equivalence implies homeomorphism. The classification is based on secondary Brown-Kervaire quadratic forms which the authors construct. For certain \(2n\)-dimensional manifolds with \(n \geq 4\), \(n \neq 3\) mod 4 they prove the existence of a quadratic function \(\phi: \;H^{n-1}(M;\mathbb Z_4) \rightarrow \mathbb Q/4\) satisfying \(\phi(x+y) = \phi(x) + \phi(y) + (x \smile Sq^2 y)[M]\), and the Witt class of \(\phi\) becomes a homotopy invariant.

hits.title: Standard zero-free regions for Rankin-Selberg \(L\)-functions via sieve theory
hits.text:
The locations and distributions of the zeros of \(L\)-functions have important arithmetic applications, so their studies have been a central topic in number theory. In particular, if an \(L\)-function \(L(s)\) is known to be automorphic with \(L(s) = L(s, \pi)\) for some unitary cuspidal automorphic representation \(\pi\) of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{A}_F)\), then it has a zero-free region of form [\textit{H. Iwaniec} and \textit{E. Kowalski}, Analytic number theory. Providence, RI: American Mathematical Society (AMS) (2004; Zbl 1059.11001)]
\[
\sigma \geq 1 - \frac{c}{(n [F : \mathbb{Q}])^4 \log\Big(q (|t| + 3)\Big)} \tag{*}
\]
for some absolute constant \(c > 0\), where \(q\) is the analytic conductor. However, the standard argument due to de la Valleé Poussin requires the meromorphic continuations of the Rankin-Selberg convolutions \(L_1(s) = L(s, \pi \times \pi)\) and \(L_2(s) = L(s, \pi \times \tilde{\pi})\) to the whole complex plane, where \(\tilde{\pi}\) is the contragradient of \(\pi\). Such analytic properties have not been established for the counterparts of \(L_1(s)\) and \(L_2(s)\) for general \(L\)-functions, so the analysis of the zero-free regions of these \(L\)-functions is much subtler and more challenging.

The paper under review considers one such case, namely the zero-free region for the Rankin-Selberg \(L\)-function \(L(s, \pi \times \tilde{\pi})\), where \(\pi\) is a unitary cuspidal automorphic representation of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{A}_F)\) over a number field \(F\), tempered at every non-Archimedean place outside a set of Dirichlet density zero. This problem has been discussed by several authors in different contexts, including \textit{S. S. Gelbart} and \textit{E. M. Lapid} [Am. J. Math. 128, No. 3, 619--638 (2006; Zbl 1142.11034)], the second author [Am. J. Math. 128, No. 6, 1455--1474 (2006; Zbl 1137.11058)], and \textit{D. Goldfeld} and \textit{X. Li} [Int. Math. Res. Not. 2018, No. 22, 7067--7136 (2018; Zbl 1440.11080)]. Using the sieve method, the authors provide a simple proof for the zero-free region of \(L(s, \pi \times \tilde{\pi})\) in the \(t\)-aspect, namely
\[
\sigma \geq 1 - \frac{c}{\log(|t| + 3)}
\]
for some constant \(c > 0\) that depends upon the automorphic representation \(\pi\).

In the appendix to this paper, the second author gives the first published proof to an often-claimed property that a Rankin-Selberg convolution \(L(s, \pi_1 \times \pi_2)\) satisfies a standard zero-free region akin to (*) whenever either \(\pi_1\) or \(\pi_2\) is self-dual (with the possible exception of one real zero whenever they are both self-dual).

hits.title: Excellent surfaces and their taut resolution
hits.source: Hauser, H. (ed.) et al., Resolution of singularities. A research textbook in tribute to Oscar Zariski. Based on the courses given at the working week in Obergurgl, Austria, September 7-14, 1997. Basel: Birkhäuser. Prog. Math. 181, 341-373 (2000).
hits.text:
In this paper the author gives a proof of resolution of singularities in the case of excellent two-dimensional schemes embedded in three-space over an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic. The centers of blowup are chosen inside the equimultiple locus, but might be non-reduced. The particular choice of the center and the resulting blow-up is called taut. The author follows Zariski in showing that one can reduce the situation to the case that the equimultiple locus is a normal crossing, and proves that this situation persists under taut blow-up. To prove that the algorithm terminates, he introduces an invariant \(i_a\) for every closed point \(a\). This invariant is an element of a well ordered subset of \({\mathbb Q}^4\). The first component is the multiplicity, the other three are orders of certain coefficient ideals associated to a defining local equation of the surface. These can be expressed with the help of the Newton polyhedron.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0932.00042].

hits.title: Quadratic Chabauty for modular curves: algorithms and examples
hits.text:
This article describes how the quadratic Chabauty method may be applied to determine the set of rational points on modular curves of genus \(g>1\) whose Jacobians have Mordell-Weil rank \(g\). This method works for modular curves that may have few known rational points or non-trivial local height contributions at primes of bad reduction. The algorithm is demonstrated for a number of modular curves determining the set of rational points. These examples include curves \(X_{S_4}(13)\), \(X_{ns}^+(17)\), \(X_{11}, X_{15}\) and the Atkin-Lehner quotient \(X_0^+(N)\) of prime level \(N\).

Theorem 1: \(\#X_{S_4}(13)(\mathbb Q)=4\). One of these points is a CM point corresponding to the discriminant \(-3\), and the other three are exceptional points.

Theorem 2: \(\# X^+_{ns}(17)(\mathbb Q)=7\). All of these points are CM points corresponding to discriminants \(-3, -7,-11,-12,-27,-28\) and \(-163\).

Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 complete the classification of the possible \(13\)-adic and \(17\)-adic images of Galois representations.

The set of rational points on the Atkin-Lehner quotient \(X_0^+(N) =X_0(N)/\langle w_N\rangle\) of the modular curve \(X_0(N)\) is also discussed with the quadratic Chabauty method.

Theorem 3: The only prime values \(N\) such that \(X_0^+(N)\) is of genus \(2\) and \(3\) and has an exceptional rational points are \(N=73, 103\) and \(191\). In particular, for prime \(N\), there are no exceptional rational points on curves \(X_0^+(N)\) of genus \(3\).

The quadratic Chabauty method has three main ingredients: the global height function \(h_V\) away from \(p\), the height function \(h_p\), and the global height pairing \(h\). The algorithm is developed to compute local heights away from \(p\), and the global height pairing.

hits.title: Borsuk's partition problem and finite point sets
hits.text:
In his famous paper [Fundam. Math. 20, 177--190 (1933; Zbl 0006.42403)], \textit{K. Borsuk} asked if every bounded subset \(X\) of \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\) can be decomposed into \(n+1\) subsets with diameters smaller than \(\operatorname{diam} X\). In this paper, the author shows that this is equivalent to a similiar question on finite subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\) or of \(\mathbb{Z}^{n}\) by a general result of the following theorem on coverings of compact metric spaces.

Let \(Y\) be a compact metric space, \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\). Then the following statements are equivalent: {\parindent=0.7cm\begin{itemize}\item[(i)] Every subset \(X \subseteq Y\) with \(\operatorname{diam}X=1 \) is the union of \( k \) subsets with diameters smaller than \( t \). \item [(ii)] Every countable subset \(X \subseteq Y\) with \( \operatorname{diam} X=1 \) is the union of \( k \) subsets with diameters smaller than \( t \). \item [(iii)] For some real number \(c<t\), every subset \(X \subseteq Y\) with \(\operatorname{diam} X=1 \) is the union of \( k \) subsets with diameters at most \( c \). \item[(iv)] For some real number \(c<t\), every finite subset \(X \subseteq Y\) with \(\operatorname{diam} X=1 \) is the union of \( k \) subsets with diameters at most \( c \). 

\end{itemize}} If these conditions hold, then one can take the same constant \( c \) in (iii) and (iv). Moreover, the author also considers Borsuk's problem in \(\mathbb{Q}^{4}\).

hits.title: On the Brauer group of diagonal quartic surfaces. With an appendix by Peter Swinnerton-Dyer
hits.source: J. Lond. Math. Soc., II. Ser. 83, No. 3, 659-672 (2011).
hits.text:
Let \(D\) be the diagonal quartic surface in \({\mathbb P}^3\) defined by the equation 
\[
x_0^4 + a_1 x_1^4 + a_2 x_2^4 + a_3 x_3^4 = 0,
\]
 where \(a_1,a_2,a_3 \in \mathbb Q^*\). In this article, the authors study the Brauer group of the surface \(D\).

The Brauer group contains two natural subgroups: the subgroup \(\mathbf{Br}_0(D) = \mathbf{Im}(\mathbf{Br}(\mathbb Q) \to \mathbf{Br}(D))\) of constant elements, and the subgroup \(\mathbf{Br}_1(D) = \mathbf{Ker}(\mathbf{Br}(D) \to \mathbf{Br}(\bar{D}))\) of algebraic elements. The importance of this article is that it addresses the transcendental elements of \(\mathbf{Br} D\), that is, those elements which do not lie in \(\mathbf{Br}_1 D\). Very little is known explicitly about transcendental Brauer groups over \(\mathbb Q\). The two results which are likely to prove very useful are the following.

Corollary 3.3. Let \(H_D \subset \mathbb Q^*\) be the subgroup generated by \(-1\), \(4\), \(a_1\), \(a_2\), \(a_3\) and the fourth powers \({\mathbb Q^*}^4\). If \(\{2,3,5\} \cap H_D = \emptyset\), then \(\mathbf{Br}(D) = \mathbf{Br}_1(D)\).

Corollary 4.6. Let \(D \subset {\mathbb P}^3_\mathbb Q\) be the quartic surface (1). Then: 
{\parindent=8mm 
\begin{itemize}\item[(i)] the exponent of the group \(\mathbf{Br}(D)/\mathbf{Br}_1(D)\) divides \(2^{10} \cdot 3 \cdot 5\); 
\item[(ii)] the order of \(\mathbf{Br}(D)/\mathbf{Br}_1(D)\) divides \(2^{20} \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5^2\); 
\item[(iii)] the order of \(\mathbf{Br}(D)/\mathbf{Br}_0(D)\) divides \(2^{25} \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5^2\). 

\end{itemize}}
(Let us note that (ii) follows from (i) since \(\mathbf{Br}(D)/\mathbf{Br}_1(D)\) is known to lie in \((\mathbb Q/{\mathbb Z})^2\) by the standard computation of the Brauer group of a smooth surface over an algebraically closed field; and (iii) follows from (ii) by known bounds for \(\mathbf{Br}_1(D)/\mathbf{Br}_0(D)\), which can be calculated using Galois cohomology.)

The results follow from the possibly surprising observation that the Fermat quartic surface (i.e., the surface \(D\) when \(a_1=a_2=a_3=1\)) is a Kummer surface, at least after a base extension. An explicit isomorphism over \(\mathbb Q(\mu_8)\) was described by Mizukami in his PhD thesis, and the details of the construction are given by Sir Peter Swinnerton-Dyer in an appendix to this paper. The Kummer surface in question is associated to an Abelian surface \(A\) which is isogenous to the product \(E \times E\), where \(E\) is the elliptic curve \(y^2 = x^3 - 4x\). The results on the Brauer group of \(D\) are obtained by relating \(\mathbf{Br} D\) to the Brauer group of the Kummer surface; a detailed calculation of the Galois representation on the torsion points of \(E\) then leads to the results.

hits.title: Number fields without universal quadratic forms of small rank exist in most degrees
hits.source: Math. Proc. Camb. Philos. Soc. 174, No. 2, 225-231 (2023).
hits.text: Let \(F\) be a totally real number field, i.e., all infinite places are real, let \(\mathcal{O}\) be its ring of algebraic integers and denote by \(\mathcal{O}^+\) the subset of all totally positive integers. Obviously, a totally positive definite quadratic \(\mathcal{O}\)-lattice (or lattice for short) only represents elements in \(\mathcal{O}^+\), and a lattice is called universal if it represents every element in \(\mathcal{O}^+\). Universal lattices exist for every totally real number field \(F\), so it is natural to ask for the smallest positive integer \(m\) such that a universal lattice (resp. free universal lattice) of rank \(m\) exists. This integer will be denoted by \(m(F)\) (resp. \(m'(F)\)). Note that \(m(F)\leq m'(F)\leq m(F)+1\), but apparently no examples of \(F\) with \(m(F)\neq m'(F)\) are known. By the Four-Square theorem and the Hasse-Minkowski theorem, one has \(m(\mathbb{Q})=4\). If \(D\geq 2\) is a square-free integer, then \(m'(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D}))\geq 3\) with equality if \(D=2,3,5\), see [\textit{W.-K. Chan} et al., Jpn. J. Math., New Ser. 22, No. 2, 263--273 (1996; Zbl 0868.11020)]. On the other hand, the present author showed that to any integer \(m>0\) there are infinitely many such \(D\) with \(m(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D}))\geq m\), [\textit{V. Kala}, Bull. Aust. Math. Soc. 94, No. 1, 7--14 (2016; Zbl 1345.11025)]. In the present paper, this result is extended significantly. It is shown that to any integers \(d,m>0\) with \(d\) divisible by \(2\) or \(3\), there exist infinitely many totally real number fields \(F\) with \([F:\mathbb{Q}]=d\) and \(m(F)\geq m\).

hits.title: Endomorphism algebras of abelian varieties
hits.source: Algebraic geometry and commutative algebra, Vol. II, 469-502 (1988).
hits.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0655.00011.] 


Suppose given a field k and a positive integer g. Which algebras D can appear as the endomorphism algebra \(D\cong End^ 0_ k(X)\) of an abelian variety X over k with \(\dim (X)=g?\) 


Albert classified all central simple algebras with a positive definite involution: there is a finite list of types of algebras which can appear in this way. - Albert, Shimura and Gerritzen showed that all these algebras can appear (if no restriction on g with respect to D is made). Moreover in characteristic zero it is completely clear which restrictions on D are necessary and sufficient for a given g. 


In this paper the situation in characteristic p is studied in case the field k is algebraically closed. One of the striking facts is that splitting/ramification behavior of p in the algebra extension \(D\supset {\mathbb{Q}}\) and the p-rank of X play an essential role. Furthermore the representations of D on the \(\ell\)-adic and on the p-adic Tate module (together with the Dieudonné-Manin theory) are used. - The strategy of the paper is as follows: on the one hand restrictions on D for given g and char(k) are studied, and on the other hand constructions and examples are given in order to show that the algebras which are not excluded by these restriction actually do appear. In most cases this works, and complete answers are derived. 


Various constructions are used. One is lifting to characteristic zero (and using the characteristic zero existence results). As in some cases in characteristic p the endomorphism algebras are bigger this does not always work. In such cases deformations of semi-abelian varieties (following Mumford and Faltings) are studied. Furthermore results about abelian varieties over finite fields (Tate, Grothendieck, Honda, Serre) are essentially used. 


In order to indicate the flavor of this field we indicate some facts and results (for a more complete survey we refer to the article): Suppose X is a simple abelian variety which has smCM (sufficiently many complex multiplications, i.e. D contains a field L with \([L:{\mathbb{Q}}]=2\cdot \dim(X))\). In characteristic zero \(D=L\) is a field. In characteristic p the same holds if the p-rank f of X equals \(g=\dim (X)\) or not, but there exist many examples of simple abelian varieties with smCM such that D is not commutative (e.g. \(X=E\) is a supersingular elliptic curve, e.g. \(\dim(X)\geq 3\) and \(End^ 0(X)\) is a division algebra of rank \(g^ 2\) over its centre F, which is a quadratic extension of \({\mathbb{Q}}\), or see proposition (5.5) where many more examples are given). 


If D is a division algebra from the list of Albert, there exists an abelian variety X such that \(End^ 0(X)\cong D\). A construction by \textit{L. Gerritzen} [Math. Ann. 194, 109-122 (1971; Zbl 0245.14016)] gives this result, with \(\dim(X)=[D:{\mathbb{Q}}]\), or \(=2\cdot [D:{\mathbb{Q}}]\). In theorem (3.4) we find that in certain cases (depending on the p-rank, D and char(k)) this is the smallest \(\dim(X)=g\) for which this is possible. 


If \(char(k)=0\), and \(End^ 0(X)\) is a quaternion algebra, then \(\dim (X)=g\) is even, however if \(char(k)=p\) this need not be true. In theorem (4.8) we find all cases which occur for a positive definite quaternion algebra over \({\mathbb{Q}}\). For example, if \([D:{\mathbb{Q}}]=4\), and D is unramified for all primes different from p (standard notation: \(D=K_{\infty,p})\), any integer \(g\geq 5\) does appear as the dimension of an abelian variety in characteristic p having exactly D as its endomorphism algebra [this uses the ideas of Gerritzen, Mumford and Faltings adopted for such cases by the author and \textit{M. van der Put} in Compos. Math. 67, No.1, 103-120 (1988; Zbl 0656.14024)].

hits.title: On Greenberg's generalized conjecture for CM-fields
hits.text:
Let \(k\) be a number field and let \(p\) be a prime. Denote the composite of all \(\mathbb Z_p\)-extensions of \(k\) by \(\tilde k\) and for any subfield \(L\) of \(\tilde k\) let \(X_L\) be the Galois group over \(L\) of the maximal unramified abelian pro-\(p\)-extension of \(L\).

If \(k\) is totally real and \(L = k_\infty\) is the cyclotomic \(\mathbb Z_p\)-extension of \(k\), \textit{R. Greenberg} [Am. J. Math. 98, 263--284 (1976; Zbl 0334.12013)] conjectured that \(X_{k_\infty}\) is a pseudo-null Iwasawa module. Note that under Leopoldt's conjecture one has \(k_\infty=\tilde k\) in this case. More generally, for an arbitrary number field \textit{R. Greenberg} [Adv. Stud. Pure Math. 30, 335--385 (2001; Zbl 0998.11054)] conjectures that the Iwasawa module \(X_{\tilde k}\) is pseudo-null.

The main result of this article is as follows. Let \(k\) be a CM-field and let \(p\) be an odd prime which splits completely in \(k/\mathbb Q\) and such that \(p\) does not divide the class number of \(k\). Let \(k^+\) be the maximal totally real subfield of \(k\). Assume that Leopoldt's conjecture holds for \(k^+\) at \(p\) and that \(X_{k_\infty^+}\) is pseudo-null. Then \(X_{\tilde k}\) is also pseudo-null.

This generalizes results of \textit{J. Minardi} [CMS Conf. Proc. 7, 237--242 (1987; Zbl 0625.12004)] and \textit{T. Itoh} [J. Number Theory 131, No. 1, 59--66 (2011;Zbl 1211.11119)] who treated the case \([k:\mathbb Q] = 2\) and \([k:\mathbb Q] = 4\), respectively. However, the proof is not independent of these results, as the authors often assumes that \([k:\mathbb Q] \geq 4\).

The proof mainly follows Itoh's approach. One defines a chain of intermediate fields \(K^{(i)} \subseteq K^{(i+1)}\), \(1 \leq i \leq m\) such that \(K^{(i)}/k\) is a sub-\(\mathbb Z_p^i\)-extension and \(K^{(m+1)} = \tilde k\), where \([k:\mathbb Q] = 2m\). Then one shows by induction that each \(X_{K^{(i)}}\) is pseudo-null using class field theory.

hits.title: Polynomial bound for the number of rational points on curves
hits.text:
Let \(k\) be a number field, with discriminant \(\Delta\). Let \(f\in k[X,Y]\) be a polynomial of degree \(D\). The main theorem of the paper states that the set of affine \(k\)-rational points of \(f(x,y)=0\) is either infinite or bounded by 
\[
 \text{exp}\left(2^{3^{D^2}}[K:{\mathbb Q}]^4 \max (h_\infty(F), \log|\Delta|, 1)\right), 
\]
 where \(h_\infty(F)\) denotes the logarithm of the maximum archimedean absolute value of the coefficients of \(F\).

The paper uses a simple estimate of the number of points of \({\mathbb P}^n(\bar{\mathbb Q})\) of degree \(\leq D\) and of height \(\leq H\) and compares with a previous paper of the same author [Proc. Lond. Math. Soc. (3) 101, No. 3, 759--794 (2010; Zbl 1210.11073)], improving the term of the estimate concerning the height but losing (substantially) on the dependence on the degree.

For a pair \((X, E)\), where \(X\) is a compact complex manifold of dimension \(n\) and \(E\) is an ample vector bundle on \(X\) of rank \(r < n\), the author defines a new genus \(g(X,E)\) by 
\[
2g(X,E) -2 = (K +(n-r) c_1) c_1^{n-r-1} c_r
\]
 where \(K\) is the canonical line bundle and \(c_1, c_r\) are respectively the first and top Chern classes of \(E\). It is shown that \(g(X,E)\) is a non-negative integer. 


Theorem. Let \(1<r<n-1\). 


(1) \(g(X,E) = 0\) if and only if \((X,E) = ({\mathbb P}^4, {\mathcal O}(1)^{\oplus 2})\).


(2) \(g(X,E) = 1\) if and only if \((X,E)\) is \(({\mathbb P}^5, {\mathcal O}(1)^{\oplus 2}), ({\mathbb P}^5, {\mathcal O}(1)^{\oplus 3})\) or \(({\mathbb Q}^4, {\mathcal O}(1)^{\oplus 2})\), where \({\mathbb Q}^4\) is a smooth hyperquadric in \({\mathbb P}^5\).


(3) If \(E\) is spanned, then \(g(X,E) \geq q(X)\), the irregularity of \(X\). Equality holds only in case \(g(X,E)=0\).


In case \(r=1\), \(g(X,E)\) coincides with the sectional genus while for \(r=n-1\), \(g(X,E)\) coincides with the curve genus defined by Ballico. Analogues of the above theorem were proved by \textit{T. Fujita} [in: Geometry of complex projective variaties, Proc. Conf., Cetraro 1990, Semin. Conf. 9, 153-163 (1993; Zbl 0937.14023)] for \(r=1\) and by \textit{A. Lanteri, H. Maeda} and \textit{A. J. Sommese} in case \(r=n-1\) [Arch. Math. 66, No.~2, 141-149 (1996; Zbl 0853.14022)].

hits.text:
The paper defines the Zariski topology-graphs of modules over commutative rings and the annihilating-submodule graphs of such modules. Let \(R\) be a commutative ring with non-zero unit and \(M\) an \(R\)-module. A prime submodule \(P\) of \(M\) is a submodule such that whenever \(rm\in P\) for \(r\in R\) and \(m\in M\), either \(m\in P\) or \(r\in (P:M)\). In such a case, \((P:M)\) is a prime ideal of \(R\). For example, maximal submodules of \(M\) are prime. The set of prime submodules of \(M\) is denoted by \(\text{Spec}(M)\), which coincides with the usual prime spectrum if \(M=R\).

The spectrum \(\text{Spec}(M)\) has a topology structure with closed sets being \(V(N)=\{P\in \text{Spec}(M): (P:M)\supseteq (N:M)\}\) where \(N\) runs through the submodules of \(M\). The Zariski topology-graph associated with a subset \(T\) of \(\text{Spec}(M)\) is then defined to be \(G(\tau_T)\) with vertices being those proper submodules \(N\subseteq M\) such that \(V(N)\neq T\) and \(V(N)\cup V(L)=T\) for some proper submodule \(L\) of \(M\) with \(V(L)\neq T\). In these conditions on \(N\) and \(L\) are satisfied, they are defined to be neighbors of each other. In Theorem 2.10, it is shown that if \(G(\tau_T)\neq \emptyset\) then it is connected of diameter \(\leq 3\), and assuming that \(G(\tau_T)\) contains a cycle, its girth is at most \(4\).

Section 3 is devoted to the annihilating-submodule graph \(AG(M)\) of \(M\). A vertex of \(AG(M)\) is a submodule \(N\) of \(M\) (possibly equal to \(M\)) such that \(LN=0\) for some non-zero proper submodule \(L\) of \(M\). Here, the product \(LN\) of two submodules is defined to be \((L:M)(N:M)M\), which is the usual product of ideals if \(M\) happens to be \(R\). Two vertices of \(AG(M)\) are adjacent if their product is zero. In Theorem 3.4, it is proved that \(AG(M)\) enjoys exactly the same properties of \(G(\tau_T)\) mentioned above.

In section 4, the authors study the relationship between \(G(\tau_T)\) and \(AG(M)\), given some condition on the submodule \(\mathcal{I}(T)=\bigcap_{P\in T}P\) of \(M\).

Reviewer's remarks: Besides the interesting results, the paper contains some minor errors/typos:

(1) In paragraph 4 of the first page, it should be mentioned that non-capital \(p\) is the ideal \(P:M\).

(2) In Section 3, paragraph 3, the formula for product of \(N\) and \(L\) should be \((N:M)(L:M)M\), not \((N:M)(K:M)M\).

(3) Line -2 before Theorem 3.3, \(N\) should be a proper submodule of \(\mathbb{Q}\).

(4) In the proof of Theorem 3.4, one should add that if \(N_3N_4\neq 0\) then we have a path \(N_1---N_3N_4---N_2\) of length \(2\).

(5) In Proposition 4.2, the correct phrase is ``for example, when \(M/\mathcal{I}(T)\) is a multiplication module'', with \(M/\mathcal{I}(T)\) in place of \(AG(M/\mathcal{I}(T))\).


For Part II, see [the authors, Arab. J. Math. 10, No. 1, 41--50 (2021; Zbl 1460.13019)].

hits.title: A Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem for higher-rank groups
hits.text:
In the paper under review, the authors establish a result of Bombieri-Vinogradov type for the Dirichlet coefficients at prime ideals of the standard \(L\)-function associated to a self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation \(\pi\) of \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) over a number field \(F\) when \(\pi\) is not a quadratic twist of itself. Actually, they prove the following:

Let \(A>0\), \(B=2^{\frac{n [F:\mathbb{Q}]}{4}}(6A+12n+34)+2n-4\) and \(\eta=\max \lbrace 2, \frac{n}{2} \rbrace\). We denote by \(\mbox{Cl}^+(\mathfrak{m})\) the narrow class group modulo \(\mathfrak{m}\) and \(N=N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}\) by the numerical norm. Let \(h(\mathfrak{m})\) be the cardinality of \(\mbox{Cl}^+(\mathfrak{m})\) and \(\varphi_F(\mathfrak{m})=N \mathfrak{m}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}|\mathfrak{m}}(1-N\mathfrak{p}^{-1})\). Then, 
\[
\sum_{N \mathfrak{m}\leq Q}\frac{h(\mathfrak{m})}{\varphi_F(\mathfrak{m})} \max_{(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{m})=\mathcal{O}_K} \max_{y\leq x}\left| \sum_{\stackrel{N \mathfrak{p}\leq y}{p\equiv \mathfrak{a}\: Cl^+ (\mathfrak{m})}} \lambda_\pi (\mathfrak{p}) \right|\ll_A \frac{x}{(\log x)^A},
\]
where \(x\geq 2\) ,\(Q=x^{\frac{1}{\eta}} (\log x)^{-B}\), and the implied constant is ineffective. As consequence, it is proven the first unconditional Siegel-type lower bound for the twisted \(L\)-values \(|L(1,\pi \otimes\chi)|\) in the \(\chi\)-aspect, where \(\chi\) is a primitive quadratic Hecke character over \(F\).

hits.title: An application of Siegel modular functions to Kronecker's limit formula
hits.source: Fieker, Claus (ed.) et al., Algorithmic number theory. 5th international symposium, ANTS-V, Sydney, Australia, July 7--12, 2002. Proceedings. Berlin: Springer (ISBN 3-540-43863-7). Lect. Notes Comput. Sci. 2369, 108-119 (2002).
hits.text:
Let \(\zeta=\exp(\frac{2\pi i}{13})\), \(\alpha=\zeta+\zeta^3+\zeta^9\) and \(k\) the unique subfield of \(\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)\) with \([k:\mathbb{Q}]=4\). It is well known that \(\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)\) is a CM-field corresponding to the Jacobian variety of a genus two curve \(C\). In this paper the authors construct a Minkowski unit \(\varepsilon\) of the ray class field \(k(6)\) of \(k\) modulo 6, by using special values of Siegel modular functions at a CM-point corresponding to the Jacobian variety of \(C\). Then, by using their result, they expressed the values of \(L\)-functions \(L(s,\chi)\) at \(s=1\) of some subfields of \(k(6)\) in terms of logarithms of units given by Siegel modular fuctions. In Math. Comput. 69, No. 231, 1207--1212 (2000; Zbl 1037.11043) and J. Th. Nombres, Bordeaux (submitted) they have proven analogous results in the case where \(\zeta=\exp(\frac{2\pi i}{5})\).

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0992.00024].

hits.title: Solutions to \(xyz=1\) and \(x+y+z=k\) in algebraic integers of small degree. II
hits.text:
Let \(k\in\mathbb Z\) and consider the system of equations 
\[
xyz = 1,\quad x + y + z = k.
\]
 The solutions \(x,y,z\) of this system of equations were first considered by Cassels over \(\mathbb Q\). Several authors considered generalizations of this problem, extending the type of the equation or considering the solutions in a ring of algebraic integers instead of \(\mathbb Z\), cf. e.g. \textit{A. Bremner} [Acta Arith. 57, No. 4, 375--385 (1991; Zbl 0686.10012)].

This paper is the continuation of the authors' work [Acta Arith. 162, No. 4, 381--392 (2014; Zbl 1358.11049)] where the correspondng curve 
\[
{\mathcal E}_k : Y^2 = 1 - 2kX + k^2X^2 - 4X^3
\]
 was defined and the authors determined all solutions of the system of equations in algebraic integers \(x,y,z\) in a field of degree at most 4, with \(k\in\mathbb Z\) such that \(|{\mathcal E}_k(\mathbb Q)|=3\).

In this work, the authors extend the results to include \(k =-1\) and \(k = 5\), and prove that this, then, solves the problem for all \(k\) with \({\mathcal E}_k(\mathbb Q)\) finite.

In Section 2, they prove that for \(k\in\mathbb Z\), if \({\mathcal E}_k(\mathbb Q)\) is finite, but not of order 3, then \(k\in \{1,-5\}\). In Section 3, all solutions to the system of equations are found with \((x,y,z)\in {\mathcal O}_F^3\) where \([F : \mathbb Q] \leq 3\) and \(k\in \{1,-5\}\). Finally, in Section 4, we they solve the case \([F : \mathbb Q] = 4\).

hits.title: Two-descent on some genus two curves
hits.text:
Consider the hyperelliptic curves of genus two, varying \(p\) a prime, \[C_p:y^2=x(x^2-p^2)(x^2-4p^2),\] which are a quadratic twist of \(y^2=x(x^2-1)(x^2-4)\) over \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{p})\) and \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})\). The authors of the paper under review investigate the arithmetic of \(C_p\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\) in terms of \(p\), in particular the rank of the Jacobian \(J_p\) of \(C_p\). The results of the paper under review are mainly the Master thesis of two of the authors supervised by the third author of the paper, corresponding to [\textit{T. Evink}, Two descent on hyperelliptic curves of genus 2. Groningen: University of Groningen (Master Thesis) (2020), \url{http://fse.studenttheses.ub.rug.nl/21636}; \textit{G.-J. van der Heiden}, Computing the 2-descent over \(\mathbb{Q}\) for curves of genus 2. Groningen: University of Groningen (Master Thesis)  (1998), \url{http://fse.studenttheses.ub.rug.nl/8657}].

In the paper under review, first, the authors compute the \(\mathbb{F}_2\)-dimension of the \(2\)-Selmer group of \(J_p\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\), denoted by \(S^2(J_p/\mathbb{Q})\), by explicit 2-descent, method described in [\textit{E. F. Schaefer}, J. Number Theory 51, No. 2, 219--232 (1995; Zbl 0832.14016)]. The result is presented in terms as \(p\) congruent to 1,5,7,11,13,17,19,23 modulo 24, and next they study the family of \(C_p\) with \(p\) congruent to a fix of such odd primes modulo 24. From the usual sequence: \[0\rightarrow J_p(\mathbb{Q})/2J_p(\mathbb{Q})\rightarrow S^2(J_p/\mathbb{Q})\rightarrow \text{Ш}(J_p/\mathbb{Q})[2]\rightarrow 0,\] where \(\text{Ш}(J_p/\mathbb{Q})[2]\) is the 2-torsion of the Tate-Shafarevich group associated to \(J_p\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\), (and because all Weierstrass points on \(C_p\) are \(\mathbb{Q}\)-rational), they prove that the torsion group of \(J_p(\mathbb{Q})\) corresponds to the group generated by the Weierstrass points. And deduce that \[\mathrm{rank}(J_p(\mathbb{Q}))+\mathrm{dim}_{\mathbb{F}_2}\text{Ш}(J_p/\mathbb{Q})[2]=\mathrm{dim}_{\mathbb{F}_2}S^2(J_p/\mathbb{Q})-4.\]

Next, the authors are interested to obtain the rank of \(J_p(\mathbb{Q})\), and the dimension of the two torsion of the Tate-Shafarevich group. To attack such questions, because the curves \(C_p\) are twists of the hyperelliptic curve \(C:y^2=x(x^2-1)(x^2-4)\), the authors observe the relation \[\mathrm{rank} J_p(\mathbb{Q})+\mathrm{rank}\, \mathrm{Jac}(C)(\mathbb{Q})=\mathrm{rank} \,\mathrm{Jac}(C)(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\pm p})),\] for both possibilities of the sign \(\pm\). By a computation of the authors in the paper under review they obtain that \(\mathrm{rank}\,(\mathrm{Jac}(C)(\mathbb{Q}))=0\), and it follows that \[\mathrm{rank}J_p(\mathbb{Q})\leq \mathrm{dim}_{\mathbb{F}_2} S^2(\mathrm{Jac}(C)/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\pm p}))-4.\] Next, the authors compute the dimension of \(S^2(\mathrm{Jac}(C)/\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\pm p}))\), computation inspired by [Evink, loc. cit.] but using Rédei symbols (recalled in the paper) instead of different reciprocity arguments in [Evink, loc. cit.]. Finally, the \(\mathbb{Q}\)-rationals points of \(C_p\) are briefly discussed, in particular the authors prove in the paper that the set \(C_{241}(\mathbb{Q})\) is the expected set, (where \(\mathrm{rank}\,\mathrm{Jac}(C_{241})(\mathbb{Q})=2\), so the standard Chabauty method does not apply to verify the computational expectation).
