hits.title: On the vanishing of the Rokhlin invariant
hits.text:
It was proven by Casson in the 1980's that the Rokhlin invariant \(\mu(M)\in \mathbb{Z}/16 \mathbb{Z}\) of an amphichiral homology \(3\)-sphere \(M\) vanishes, (see e.g. [\textit{S. Akbulut} and \textit{J. D. McCarthy}, Casson's invariant for oriented homology 3-spheres. An exposition. Mathematical Notes, 36. Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press. (1990; Zbl 0695.57011)]). In the article under review, a new proof of this theorem is presented.

A manifold \(M\) is called amphichiral, if it admits an orientation-reversing self-homeomorphism. The Rokhlin invariant of a closed oriented spin 3-manifold is defined as \(\mu(M)=\text{Sign\;} X\;(\text{mod\;}16)\), where \(X\) is a compact spin 4-manifold with boundary \(M\). If \(H^1(M,\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})=0\), then the spin structure on \(M\) is unique, and thus the Rokhlin invariant depends only on the diffeomorphism type of \(M\).

The new proof uses \(e\)-manifolds which were already introduced and studied in [\textit{T. Moriyama}, J. Math. Sci., Tokyo 18, No. 2, 193--237 (2011; Zbl 1259.57008)]. An \(n\)-dimensional \(e\)-manifold is a triple \((W,V,e)\) where \(W\) is an \(n\)-dimensional compact manifold, possibly with boundary, and where \(V\) is a submanifold of codimension \(3\), such that \(\partial V=V\cap \partial W\) with transversal intersection. Furthermore, \(e\) is a class in \(H^2(W\setminus V; \mathbb{Q})\) such that the restriction of \(e\) to a sphere in the normal bundle of \(V\) in \(W\) is the Euler class of this sphere. The relevant \(e\)-manifolds in the article carry spin structures, i.e.\ a spin structure on \(V\) and \(W\). A rational-valued invariant \(\sigma(\alpha)\) was defined in [loc. cit.] for 6-dimensional \(e\)-manifolds \(\alpha\). If \(\alpha\) is the boundary of the \(7\)-dimensional \(e\)-manifold \(\beta=(Z,X,e)\), then \(\sigma(\partial \beta)= \text{Sign\;} X\).

The author associates to every homology \(3\)-sphere \(M\) a \(6\)-dimensional spin \(e\)-manifold \(\alpha_M\). He shows that \(\alpha_M\) is the boundary of a \(7\)-dimensional \(e\)-manifold, and thus \(\mu(M)= \sigma(\alpha_M) (\text{mod\;}16)\). On the other hand \(\sigma(\alpha_{-M})= - \sigma(\alpha_M)\), and hence \(\sigma(\alpha_M)\) and \(\mu(M)\) vanish for amphichiral homology spheres.

The author also defines bordims classes \(\Omega_n^{e,\text{spin}}\) of \(n\)-dimensional closed spin \(e\)-manifolds, and he shows that there is a unique isomorphism \(\Phi:\Omega_6^{e,\text{spin}}\to \mathbb{Q}/16\mathbb{Z}\oplus \mathbb{Q}/4\mathbb{Z}\) such that 
\[
\Phi([W,\emptyset,e])=\left(\frac16\int_W p_1(TW)e-e^3,\frac12 \int_W e^3\right).
\]
 This bordism class nicely fits into an exact sequence 
\[
0\to \Omega_4^{\text{spin}}(BSpin(3))\to \Omega_6^{\text{spin}}(K(\mathbb{Q},2))\to \Omega_6^{e,\text{spin}}\to 0
\]
 which is studied further.

The article is very well-written and can be read fluently. The new proof of the vanishing of the Rokhlin invariant is according to the author more direct than previous proofs.

hits.title: On the smallest point on a diagonal quartic threefold
hits.text:
The main object of the paper under review is a diagonal quartic threefold \(V\) defined over the field of rational numbers \(\mathbb Q\). The authors are interested in getting an a priori upper bound for the height of the smallest rational point on \(V\) (such a bound would allow one to make an effective search for counter-examples to the Hasse principle). As \(V\) is a Fano variety, assuming Manin's conjectural asymptotics for rational points of bounded height (with leading term \(\tau (V)\) proposed by \textit{E.~Peyre} [Duke Math. J. 79, No. 1, 101--218 (1995; Zbl 0901.14025)]), one could expect the point of smallest height to be of order \(1/\tau (V)\).

Although computer experiments made by the authors gave some evidence in support of this expectation, their first result is negative: for \(V\) varying in the family \(ax^4=y^4+z^4+v^4+w^4\), \(a\in \mathbb N\), the smallest height of a rational point cannot be uniformly bounded by \(C/\tau(V)\). In a more positive sense, they prove the following finiteness property: for a given \(B>0\) there are only finitely many \(V\subset \mathbb P_{\mathbb Q}^4\) of the form \(a_0x_0^4+\dots +a_4x_4^4=0\) with \(a_0<0\), \(a_1,\dots ,a_4>0\) such that \(1/\tau (V)>B\).

hits.title: Generators and integral points on twists of the Fermat cubic
hits.text:
For an integer \(m\) consider the elliptic curve \(C_m: x^3+y^3=m\) and the corresponding Diophantine equation \(x^3+y^3=m\). An integer solution of the last equation is, by abuse of terminology, called ``an integral point of \(C_m\)''.

Let \(m\) be a positive cube-free integer and let \(C_m(\mathbb{Q})\) denote the Mordell-Weil group of \(C_m\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\). Note that \(C_m\) is birationally equivalent over \(\mathbb{Q}\) to the elliptic curve \(E_m: y^2=x^3-432m^2\) and, if \(m>2\), the are no non-trivial torsion points.

The purpose of this paper is to prove the following interesting results:

1. If \(P_1\in C_m(\mathbb{Q})\) is an integral point, then \(P_1\) can be in a system of generators for \(C_m(\mathbb{Q})\). In particular, if the rank of \(C_m/\mathbb{Q}\) is one, then \(P_1\) generates \(C_m(\mathbb{Q})\).

2. (Corollary). If the rank of \(C_m/\mathbb{Q}\) is one, then \(C_m\) has at most two integral points, either of which generates \(C_m(\mathbb{Q})\).

3. If \(P_1,P_2\in C_m(\mathbb{Q})\) are integrals points, such that \(P_1\neq \pm P_2\), then \(P_1,P_2\) can be in a system of generators for \(C_m(\mathbb{Q})\). In particular, if the rank of \(C_m/\mathbb{Q}\) is two, then \(P_1,P_2\) generate \(C_m(\mathbb{Q})\).

4. (Corollary). If the rank of \(C_m/\mathbb{Q}\) is two, then \(C_m\) has at most six integral points, which can be expressed as \(\pm P_1,\pm P_2,\pm (P_1+P_2)\) with generators \(P_1,P_2\) for \(C_m(\mathbb{Q})\).

5. If the rank of \(C_m/\mathbb{Q}\) is \(r\), then \(C_m\) has at most \(3^r-1\) integral points.

The proof is based on a sharp uniform lower bound for the canonical height \(\hat{h}(P)\) of any rational point on \(E_m\), which improves a similar bound due to T.~Jȩdrzejak. An even better bound due to \textit{P. Voutier} and \textit{M. Yabuta}, is published in [Int. J. Number Theory 9, No. 5, 1141--1170 (2013; Zbl 1304.11048)], which appeared after the submission of the present paper but, most likely, this wouldn't improve the main results 1-5, above.

hits.title: Formality criteria in terms of higher Whitehead brackets
hits.text:
In rational homotopy theory, one often considers \textit{formal} spaces, i.e. those whose rational homotopy type is determined by their cohomology algebra (equivalently, the minimal model can be constructed only knowing the cohomology of the given space, i.e. it is a ``formal'' consequence of the cohomology). As a way of showing that a space is not formal, one can hope to detect the existence of (higher) Massey products.

In the present paper, the authors consider the (in a sense) dual notion of coformality. A space (we will assume simply connected throughout, as the authors do, and finite type for the most part) is \textit{coformal} if its rational homotopy type is determined by the Lie algebra structure on \(\pi_*(\Omega X) \otimes \mathbb{Q}\) given by the Samelson bracket (or equivalently, up to a degree shift, by the Whitehead bracket on \(\pi_*(X) \otimes \mathbb{Q}\)). They give a proof of the folklore result that the higher Whitehead brackets, the analogues of the higher Massey products in the previous paragraph, are obstructions to coformality.

One can consider stronger versions of the above two notions, namely \textit{intrinsic} formality and coformality. A space is \textit{intrinsically formal} if it is rationally homotopy equivalent to any other space with isomorphic rational cohomology algebra; it is \textit{intrinsically coformal} if its is rationally homotopy equivalent to any other space with isomorphic rational homotopy Lie algebra. Really, these should be thought of as properties of a (Lie) algebra; intrinsic (co)formality is then rigidity in the deformation theoretic setup of Schlessinger-Stasheff. The authors give conditions under which the product of odd dimensional spheres (other than circles) is intrinsically coformal; as a special case, the product of at most four such spheres is intrinsically coformal.

Next, the authors discuss a spectral sequence due to Quillen, which collapses when applied to coformal spaces. As the authors point out, it was generally accepted that the collapse of the spectral sequence does not guarantee coformality, and they provide the first explicit example of this failure of the converse; their example in fact has all higher Whitehead products vanishing. The space considered is the total space of the \(K(\mathbb{Q}, 7)\) bundle over \(K(\mathbb{Q}, 2) \times K(\mathbb{Q}, 4)\) where the degree 7 generator of the fiber kills the square of the generator of \(K(\mathbb{Q}, 2)\) times the generator of \(K(\mathbb{Q}, 4)\). This presentation gives us a minimal model of the total space, which has cubic differential. Generally, a space is coformal if its differential is purely quadratic in some minimal model. The authors show that there is no automorphism of the model which would make the differential quadratic, hence showing the considered space is not coformal.

The authors then discuss the relationship between the higher terms in the differential of a dga model of a space and higher Whitehead products, extending work of Andrews-Arkowitz.

The interested reader is encouraged to also see the later paper [\textit{U. Buijs} et al., Mediterr. J. Math. 17, No. 1, Paper No. 31, 15 p. (2020; Zbl 1439.55020)] which complements the present one.

hits.title: Imaginary quadratic fields \(F\) with \(X_0(15)(F)\) finite
hits.text:
The paper establishes explicit conditions on a prime number \(p\) such that the elliptic curve \(X_0(15)\) has rank zero over the quadratic imaginary field \(F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})\). The authors also showed that these conditions are satisfied if and only if rank \(0\) follows from a \(4\)-descent over \(\mathbb{Q}\) on the quadratic twist \(X_0(15)_{-p}\). The bounds for the rank obtained by two consecutive \(2\)-descents proved to be equivalent to the one's obtained from a \(4\)-descend using visualization on the Shafarevitch group \(\Sha[2]\).

Theorem: Let \(p\) be a prime number satisfying one of the following conditions.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] \(p \leq 5\),
\item[(ii)] \(p \equiv 1, 2, 4, 8 \, \, \text{mod} \, \, 15\) and \(p \not \equiv 1 \, \text{mod} \, \, 8\),
\item[(iii)] \(p \equiv 1, 4 \, \, \text{mod} \, \, 15\), \(p \equiv 1 \, \text{mod} \, \, 8\) and \([-1, 10, p] =-1\),
\item[(iv)] \(p \equiv 2, 8 \, \, \text{mod} \, \, 15\), \(p \equiv 1 \, \text{mod} \, \, 8\) and \([-1, 2, p] =1\).
\end{itemize}
Then \(X_0(15)\) has rank zero over the field \(F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})\).

The Rédei symbol \([a, b, c]\), used in some of the conditions, is a trilinear number theoretic symbol taking values in \(\{\pm 1\}\) that encodes splitting behavior of rational primes in certain extensions. For example it can be shown the following:

If \( p \equiv 1, 9 \, \, \text{mod} \, \, 40\), then 
\[
 [-1, 10, p] =1 \iff p \text{ splits completely in } \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3 + \sqrt{-1}}).
\]
Also, if \( p \equiv 1 \, \, \text{mod} \, \, 8\), then 
\[
[-1, 2, p] =1 \iff p \text{ splits completely in } \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{1 + \sqrt{-1}}).
\]
As a an application of the work of \textit{A. Caraiani} and \textit{J. Newton} [``On the modularity of elliptic curves over imaginary quadratic fields'', Preprint, \url{arXiv:2301.10509}], the result in Theorem 1 implies the modularity of elliptic curves over the field \(F\). That is:

Corollary: Let \(p\) be a prime satisfying one of conditions of Theorem 1. Then every elliptic curve defined over \(F=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})\) is modular.

The following results are also proven:

Theorem: Let \(p \equiv 1, 49 \text{ mod } 120\) be a prime and let \(E\) be the modular elliptic curve \( X_0(15)\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] If \([-1, 10, p] = -1\), then \(\text{rank}(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q}))=0\) and the group 
\[
\Sha(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q})[4]) = ( \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2.
\]
\item[(ii)] If \([-1, 10, p] = 1\), then the multiplication by two map 
\[
\Sha(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q})[4]) \longrightarrow \Sha(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q})[2])
\]
is surjective.
\item[(iii)] If \([-1, 10, p] = 1\) and \(\text{rank}(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q}))=0\), then the group 
\[
\Sha(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q}))[4] = ( \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})^2.
\]
\end{itemize}

Theorem: Let \(p \equiv 17, 113 \text{ mod } 120\) be a prime and let \(E\) be the modular elliptic curve \( X_0(15)\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] If \([-1, 2, p] = 1\), then \(\text{rank}(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q}))=0\) and the Shafarevich group 
\[
\Sha(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q})[4]) = ( \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2.
\]
\item[(ii)] If \([-1, 2, p] = -1\), then the multiplication by two map 
\[
\Sha(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q})[4]) \longrightarrow \Sha(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q})[2])
\]
is surjective.
\item[(iii)] If \([-1, 2, p] = -1\) and \(\text{rank}(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q}))=0\), then we have that the group 
\[
\Sha(E_{-p}(\mathbb{Q}))[4] = ( \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})^2.
\]
\end{itemize}

hits.title: Some counterexamples for a version of Springer's theorem on forms of higher degree
hits.source: Finite Fields Appl. 107, Article ID 102646, 15 p. (2025).
hits.text:
Let \(F\) be a field, \(L/F\) a finite extension, and \(\varphi \) a form (homogeneous polynomial) of degree \(d\) in \(n \ge 2\) variables over \(F\). We call \(\varphi \) anisotropic over \(F\), if the equality \(\varphi (x \sb 1, \dots , x \sb n) = 0\) with \(x \sb i \in F\) implies \(x \sb 1 \dots x \sb n = 0\); otherwise \(\varphi \) is called isotropic. When \(\varphi \) is anisotropic over \(F\) and \(d = 2\), i.e., \(\varphi \) is a quadratic form, by \textit{T. A. Springer}'s theorem [C. R. Acad. Sci., Paris 234, 1517--1519 (1952; Zbl 0046.24303)], and Corollary 18.5 in: [\textit{R. Elman} et al., The algebraic and geometric theory of quadratic forms. Providence, RI: American Mathematical Society (AMS) (2008; Zbl 1165.11042)], \(\varphi \) remains anisotropic over \(L\) whenever the degree \([L\colon F]\) is an odd number. Special cases of Springer's theorem have earlier been used by \textit{E. Artin} and \textit{O. Schreier} to develop the theory of ordered fields, on the basis of their characterization as formally real fields (see [Abh. Math. Semin. Univ. Hamb. 5, 225--231 (1927; JFM 53.0144.01)], and Chapter XI of [\textit{S. Lang}, Algebra. 3rd revised ed. New York, NY: Springer (2002; Zbl 0984.00001)]). Similarly, it is known that if \(M/F\) is a field extension of degree \(d\) coprime to \([L\colon F]\) and \(\varphi = \alpha x \sb 0 \sp d + \nu \sb {M/F}(x \sb 1, \dots , x \sb d)\), where \(\alpha \) is a fixed element of \(F\) and \(\nu \sb {M/F}\) is the norm form of \(M/F\) with respect to a fixed basis of \(M\) over \(F\) (so \(n = d + 1\) if \(\alpha \neq 0\), and \(n = d\), otherwise), then \(\varphi \) is anisotropic over \(L\) in case it is anisotropic over \(F\); the proof relies on the fact that the equality \(\gcd (d, [L\colon F]) = 1\) ensures that the tensor product \(M \otimes \sb F L\) is a field.

The paper under review considers the following two questions, posed under the hypothesis that \(d\) and \([L\colon F]\) are coprime, and \(\varphi \) is anisotropic and irreducible:

(Q1) Does \(\varphi \) remain anisotropic over \(L\)?

(Q2) Does \(\varphi \) remain anisotropic over \(L\) if \(\varphi \) is diagonal, i.e., \(\varphi (x \sb 1, \dots x \sb n) = \sum \sb {j=1} \sp n a \sb jx \sb j \sp n\)?

If the answer is negative, we say that \(\varphi \) provides a counterexample to (Springer's theorem) of type \((L/F, d, n)\). If in addition \(\varphi \) is diagonal, then the type is denoted by \((L/F, d, n) \sb {\mathrm{diag}}\). A counterexample \(\sum \sb {i=1} \sp n a \sb ix \sb i \sp d\) to \((L/F, d, n) \sb {\mathrm{diag}}\) is called essential if the truncated form \(\sum \sb {(1 \le i \le n, i \neq j)} a \sb ix \sb i \sp n\) is anisotropic over \(L\), for each index \(j\). Otherwise the counterexample is called inessential.

The author recalls that the answers to both questions are positive if \(n = 2\), as well as in case \(d = 3\) and \([L\colon F] = 2\) (see, e.g., Exercise 28 in Chapter V of [\textit{S. Lang}, Algebra. 3rd revised ed. New York, NY: Springer (2002; Zbl 0984.00001)]). The main result of the paper under review concerning (Q1) states that if \([L\colon F] = 3\), char\((F) \neq 2\), and there is an anisotropic quadratic form \(\rho \) in \(n\) variables over \(F\), then:

(1) There exists a counterexample of type \((L/F, 4, n)\), provided that \(n \ge 3\); in particular, this is the case of \(F = \mathbb{Q}\) and any \(n \ge 3\).

(2) There exists a counterexample of type \((L/F, 8, n + 1)\) if \(n \ge 2\); in particular, this holds for \(n = 2\) and any finite field of odd characteristic, and also, for \(n = 2\) and \(F = \mathbb{Q}\).

The research on (Q2) of the present paper concentrates on the case where \(F = \mathbb{Q}\). The author introduces the notion of a \(p\)-admissible counterexample of type \((L/F, d, n) \sb {\mathrm{diag}}\) with respect to a prime \(p\), which allows him to consider (Q2) relying on elementary properties of reductions modulo \(p\) of suitably chosen polynomials with integral coefficients. Here one of the main results of the paper states that if \(L = \mathbb{Q}(\alpha )/\mathbb{Q}\) is a cubic extension, such that \(\alpha \sp 3 + a\alpha + b = 0\), \(a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\), and the polynomial \(t \sp 3 + at + b\) is irreducible modulo \(5\), then:

(1) There exists a \(5\)-admissible counterexample of type \((L/\mathbb{Q}, 4, 4) \sb {\mathrm{diag}}\). When \(a = b = 1\), there exists an essential \(5\)-admissible counterexample of this type.

(2) If \(a = 1, b = -4\), then there exists a \(5\)-admissible essential counterexample of type \((L/\mathbb{Q}, 4, 3) \sb {\mathrm{diag}}\), and an inessential \(5\)-admissible counterexample of type \((L/\mathbb{Q}, 4, 4) \sb {\mathrm{diag}}\).

The paper poses some open questions on special cases of (Q2) and contains several related results.

hits.title: A new number field construction of the lattice \(E_8\)
hits.text:
In the present paper an \(n\)-dimensional lattice \(\Lambda\) is a discrete subgroup of \(\mathbb R^n\) of rank \(n\). Lattices can be constructed from a number field \(F\) by considering geometric representations of integral ideals in \(\mathfrak O_F\) , the ring of integers of \(F\), see for instance [\textit{J. H. Conway} and \textit{N. J. A. Sloane}, Sphere packings, lattices and groups. With additional contributions by E. Bannai, R. E. Borcherds, J. Leech, S. P. Norton, A. M. Odlyzko, R. A. Parker, L. Queen and B. B. Venkov. Grundlehren der Mathematischen Wissenschaften 290. New York, NY: Springer. (1999; Zbl 0915.52003)]. If \(\Lambda\) is a lattice obtained from a number field \(F\), we say that \(\Lambda\) can be realized as an \(\mathfrak O_F\)-lattice.

\textit{M. Craig} [Mathematika 25, 44--56 (1978; Zbl 0395.10038)] showed that the \textit{\(E_8\) lattice} can be obtained from properly chosen integral ideals in rings of cyclotomic integers. \textit{E. Bayer-Fluckiger} [in: Algebraic geometry: Hirzebruch 70. Proceedings of the algebraic geometry conference in honor of F. Hirzebruch's 70th birthday. Providence, RI: American Mathematical Society. Contemp. Math. 241, 69--84 (1999; Zbl 0951.11016)] showed that \(E_8\) can be realized as an \(\mathfrak O_F\) lattice for \(F=\mathbb Q(\zeta_{15}), \mathbb Q(\zeta_{20})\) and \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{24})\). An important open problem stated in [Zbl 0951.11016] is: Given a lattice \(\Lambda\), is there a number field \(K\) such that \(\Lambda\) is an \(\mathfrak O\)-lattice? In this paper the authors prove that \(E_8\) can be realized as an \(\mathfrak O_F\)-lattice where \(F\) is a subfield of the cyclotomic field \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{pq} )\) for infinitely many properly chosen pairs \((p, q)\) of odd primes. More precisely, they prove:

There are infinitely many pairs \((p, q)\) of primes such that the lattice \(E_8\) can be realized as an \(\mathfrak O_M\)-lattice where \(M = K_1K_2\) is a subfield of \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_{pq} )\) with \(K_1\subset \mathbb Q(\zeta_p), K_2 \subset Q(\zeta_q ), [K_1 : \mathbb Q] = 4\), and \([K_2 : \mathbb Q] = 2\). For this, it suffices that \(p\) and \(q\) satisfy the conditions \(\mathrm{ord}_p q \equiv \mathrm{ord}_q p \equiv 1 \mod 2\) and be of the form \(4h_ p + 1\) and \(2h_q + 1\), respectively, where \(h_p\) and \(h_q\) are odd integers.

hits.title: Hilbert specialization results with local conditions
hits.text:
Let \(k(T)\) be a rational function field with \(k\) a field of characteristic \(0\). A \textit{specialization} at \(t_0\in {\mathbb P}^1(k)\) of a finite extension \(E/k(T)\) of degree \(n\) is a \(k\)-étale algebra of degree \(n\), that is, a finite product \(\prod_i F_i/k\) of finite extensions of \(k\) such that \(\sum_i [F_i:k]=n\). This paper deals with the construction of specialization points such that the specialization of \(E/k(T)\) at \(t_0\) consists of a single degree \(n\) field extension \(E_{t_0}/k\) and the extension \(E_{t_0}/k\) has specific local behavior. The unramified case was approached in [\textit{P. Dèbes} and the author, Adv. Stud. Pure Math. 63, 141--162 (2012; Zbl 1321.11114)] and the ramified one in [the author, Isr. J. Math. 214, No. 2, 621--650 (2016; Zbl 1380.12004)] in the special case where the extension \(E/k(T)\) is \(k\)-regular, that is, when \(E/k(T)\) is a geometric extension.

The main objective of the paper is two fold. First, it deals with the ramified case for arbitrary finite extensions and, second, it provides unifying results. In this way, it is proved that if \(k\) is Hilbertian and if \(\{t_1,\ldots, t_r\}\subseteq {\mathbb P}^1(\bar{k})\) is its branch point set, then for infinitely many points \(t_0\in {\mathbb P}^1(k)\setminus \{t_1,\ldots, t_r\}\), the specialization of \(E/k(T)\) at \(t_0\) consists of a single degree \(n\) field extension \(E_{t_0}/k\) and the set of ramification indices of \(E_{t_0}/k\) at each \({\mathcal P}\in{\mathcal S}\) is the set of all lengths of disjoint cycles involved in the decomposition of \(v(g_{i_{\mathcal P}}^{a_{\mathcal P}})\). Here \({\mathcal S}\) is certain finite set and \(g_{i_{\mathcal P}}^{a_{\mathcal P}}\) (\({\mathcal P}\in{\mathcal S}\)) generates the inertia group at \({\mathcal P}\). Sometimes the Hilbertianity assumption can be relaxed (Theorem 4.3). The non-Galois case is treated in Theorem 4.2

Section 5 provides a unifying result in the number field case (Theorem 5.1). The result for the special case \(k={\mathbb Q}\) is the following. Let \(E/{\mathbb Q}(T)\) be a finite extension of degree \(n\) with at least one \({\mathbb Q}\)-rational branch point and such that the Galois closure \(\hat{E}/{\mathbb Q}(T)\) is \({\mathbb Q}\)-regular. Then there exist three positive constants \(m_0,\alpha\) and \(\beta\) satisfying the following. Given two disjoint finite sets \({\mathcal S}_{ \mathrm{ur}}\) and \({\mathcal S}_{\mathrm{ra}}\) of prime numbers \(p\geq m_0\), there exist rational numbers \(t_0\) such that: (1) the specialization of \(E/{\mathbb Q}(T)\) at \(t_0\) consists of a single degree \(n\) extension \(E_{t_0}/{\mathbb Q}\) and \(\mathrm{ Gal}(\hat{E}_{t_0}/{\mathbb Q})=\mathrm{Gal}(\hat{E}/k(T))\); (2) no prime \(p\in {\mathcal S}_{\mathrm{ur}}\) ramifies in \(E_{t_0} /{\mathbb Q}\); (3) each prime number \(p\in {\mathcal S}_{\mathrm{ra}}\) ramifies in \(E_{t_0}/{\mathbb Q}\); (4) if \(d_{E_{t_0}}\) is the discriminant of \(E_{t_0}/{\mathbb Q}\), then \(\prod_{p\in {\mathcal S}_{\mathrm{ra}}} p \leq |d_{E_{t_0}}|\leq \alpha \prod_{p\in {\mathcal S}_{\mathrm{ur}} \cup {\mathcal S}_{\mathrm{ra}}} p^{\beta}\).

But if \(Z\) is a Fano 3-fold, and \(A\) is very ample, then the author shows that for \(Z\neq \mathbb{Q}^3\), \(X\) is a \(\mathbb{Q}^4\)-fibration over \(\mathbb{P}^1\).

hits.title: On the construction of algebraic curves by means of complex multiplication
hits.source: Berlin: TU Berlin, Fakultät II -- Mathematik und Naturwissenschaften (Diss.). iv, 147~p., open access (2010).
hits.text: Summary: Let $k$ be an imaginary quadratic number field and $\mathcal{O}_{t}$ be the order with the conductor $t$ and the discriminant $D_{t}$. We show by means of the theory of complex multiplication that the singular values of quotients of some theta functions generate the ring class field $\Omega_{t}$ modulo $t$ over $k$. This enables more efficient computation of the class polynomials of these rings class fields than the construction of class polynomials by means of quotients of values of Dedekind $\eta-$function. Furthermore, we prove that the generalised $\eta-$ quotients can be represented by quotients of Thetanullwerte. Also these representations allow us to compute the class polynomials more efficiently. In the case that $D_{t}$ satisfies certain congruence conditions, we prove that these singular values are units in the corresponding ring class fields. This property is used to compute the unit group of those ring class fields with the help of explicitely given roots of the class polynomials, which are predetermined during the construction of such polynomials. Let $(A,E)$ be a simple principally polarised abelian surface of primitive CM-type $(K,\Phi)$ with $[K:\mathbb Q]=4$. We generalise the CM-construction of hyperelliptic curves of genus two over finite fields using a condition on the Steinitz class to all primitive CM-fields. We extend the methode of elliptic curves that tests whether a singular value of an aritmetical modular function $g(\tau)$ is a generator of rings class field $\Omega_{t}$ to simple abelian varieties by using the two-dimensional reciprocity law of Shimura, the theory of complex multiplication of abelian varieties and an arithmetic of Siegel modular functions $g$ of level $(2N,4N)$, $\mbox{gcd}(2,N)=1$. This enables to introduce an algorithm, which tests whether a system of values of Siegel modular functions $g_{1}(\tau),\ g_{2}(\tau)$ and $g_{3}(\tau)$ of level $(2N,4N)$ with $\tau\in\mathbb{H}_{2}$ generate the unramified abelian extension of the reflex field $K^{r}$ of $K$ by the first main theorem of complex multiplication. At the end, the examples of some class polynomials are given together with the subgroups of the unit group of the corresponding ring class fields, which we compute with the help of singular values of the quotients of Thetanullwerte.
